classes.name: i.i.d. noise
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M8 24 C12 15 26 14 33 24 C26 34 12 33 8 24 Z"/><path d="M33 24 L43 16 L41 24 L43 32 Z"/><path d="M20 17 C22 20 22 28 20 31"/><circle cx="14" cy="22" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="9" cy="11" r="2.2"/></svg>
classes.motto: A memory like a goldfish: every draw forgets the last.
classes.title: i.i.d. noise
classes.blurb: Independent draws: the null against which all structure is measured.

card.description: Independent, identically distributed standard Gaussian draws. The reference null: no temporal structure of any order, and a Gaussian marginal.
card.simulation: Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\): the standard Gaussian distribution

card.description: Independent draws from a uniform distribution, the flattest bounded marginal.
card.simulation: Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\mathcal{U}[-1, 1]\): the uniform distribution on \([-1, 1]\)

card.description: Independent draws from the Laplace (double-exponential) distribution, with a sharper peak and heavier tails than the Gaussian.
card.simulation: Unit scale (\(b = 1\)). Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(b\): the scale of the Laplace distribution

card.description: Independent Student-t draws. Small \(\nu\) gives heavy, power-law tails; \(\nu \to \infty\) recovers the Gaussian.
card.simulation: \(\nu \in \{3, 4, 5, 7\}\) in this profile, so every instance has finite variance. Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_\nu\): Student's t distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom; \(p(x)\): its density

card.description: Independent draws from right-skewed distributions (gamma, log-normal, chi-square).
card.simulation: Gamma shape \(k\) log-uniform on [0.3, 3]; log-normal \(\sigma\) uniform on [0.3, 1.5]; chi-square \(k \in \{1, \dots, 4\}\). Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\mathrm{Gamma}(k, 1)\): gamma distribution with shape \(k\) and unit scale
\(\mathrm{LogNormal}(0, \sigma^2)\): \(e^{Z}\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\)
\(\chi^2_k\): chi-square distribution with \(k\) degrees of freedom

card.description: Independent draws from a two-component Gaussian mixture, so the marginal has two modes but there is no temporal structure.
card.simulation: Separation \(\Delta\) uniform on [2, 5] SD, weight \(w\) uniform on [0.2, 0.5]. Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(w\): the weight of the second component
\(\Delta\): the separation of the two components, in standard deviations

card.description: Independent draws from an exponential (light, one-sided tail) or a Pareto distribution (power-law tail).
card.simulation: Pareto tail index \(\alpha\) log-uniform on [2.2, 4], so the variance is finite; \(x_{\min} = 1\). Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\): the unit-rate exponential distribution
\(\alpha\): the Pareto tail index; \(x_{\min}\): its scale (the smallest value)

card.description: Heavy-tailed white noise that still has finite variance, either Student-t or a Gaussian scale mixture that occasionally draws from a much wider Gaussian.
card.simulation: Student-t \(\nu\) stratified over [3, 6] (even instances); mixture weight \(p\) uniform on [0.02, 0.1] (odd instances). Best of 12 independent draws; the realization whose empirical distribution is closest (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance) to the target law is kept.
references: Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan (1994). Continuous Univariate Distributions, Vol. 1, 2nd ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_\nu\): Student's t distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom
\(p\): the probability of a draw from the wide component (standard deviation 5)

classes.name: Linear Gaussian
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M5 26 C13 26 16 7 24 7 C32 7 35 26 43 26 Z"/><path d="M16 26 C14 30 18 33 16 37 C14 40 17 42 16 44"/><path d="M24 26 C22 30 26 33 24 37 C22 40 25 42 24 44"/><path d="M32 26 C30 30 34 33 32 37 C30 40 33 42 32 44"/></svg>
classes.motto: The jellyfish drifts in a Gaussian bell, forever relaxing back to rest.
classes.title: linear Gaussian, short memory
classes.blurb: Gaussian processes fully described by a short-memory autocorrelation.

card.description: The first-order autoregressive process, the discrete-time analogue of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The autocorrelation decays geometrically, as \(\phi^k\); negative \(\phi\) gives an alternating, blue-noise character.
card.simulation: \(\phi\) stratified over (−0.98, 0.98); a 2000-sample burn-in is discarded.
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise), variance \(\sigma^2\)
\(\phi\): the autoregressive coefficient
\(\rho(k)\): the autocorrelation at lag \(k\)

card.description: Second-order autoregression. With complex characteristic roots it is a damped stochastic oscillator with a pseudo-period; with two real roots it is a sum of two relaxations.
card.simulation: Half the instances have complex roots (pseudo-period \(P\) stratified over [3, 80] samples, modulus \(r\) over [0.5, 0.99]), half have two real roots.
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(\phi_1, \phi_2\): the autoregressive coefficients
\(r e^{\pm i\omega}\): the complex roots of the characteristic polynomial, with modulus \(r\) and angle \(\omega\)
\(P\): the pseudo-period, in samples

card.description: Higher-order autoregressions with rich, multi-peaked spectra.
card.simulation: Order \(p \in \{3, \dots, 12\}\). Coefficients are built from reflection (partial autocorrelation) coefficients drawn uniformly on (−0.8, 0.8) via the Levinson–Durbin recursion, which guarantees stationarity; redrawn until the slowest mode decays within about 30 samples (spectral radius ≤ 0.97).
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(p\): the order; \(\phi_k\): the autoregressive coefficients

card.description: Moving-average processes, whose autocorrelation is exactly zero beyond lag \(q\).
card.simulation: \(q \in \{1, \dots, 10\}\), \(\theta_j = u_j r^j\) with \(u_j\) uniform on (−1, 1) and \(r\) on [0.5, 0.95]. Non-invertible cases are allowed.
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(q\): the order; \(\theta_j\): the moving-average coefficients

card.description: Mixed autoregressive moving-average processes, the general finite-parameter linear Gaussian model.
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(\phi_k\): autoregressive coefficients (order \(p\)); \(\theta_j\): moving-average coefficients (order \(q\))

card.description: A multiplicative seasonal autoregression, with dependence at lag 1 and at a seasonal lag \(s\). Its autocorrelation has peaks at multiples of \(s\).
equations: (1 - \phi B)(1 - \Phi B^{s})\, x_t = \varepsilon_t, \quad \text{i.e.} \quad x_t = \phi\, x_{t-1} + \Phi\, x_{t-s} - \phi\Phi\, x_{t-s-1} + \varepsilon_t
card.simulation: Season \(s\) stratified over [4, 60] samples, \(\Phi\) uniform on [0.5, 0.95], \(\phi\) uniform on [−0.5, 0.5].
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(s\): the seasonal lag; \(\Phi\): the seasonal coefficient; \(\phi\): the lag-1 coefficient
\(B\): the backshift operator, \(B x_t = x_{t-1}\)

card.description: Gaussian noise band-pass filtered around a center frequency, a random quasi-oscillation whose phase and amplitude wander.
equations: x_t = (h * \varepsilon)_t, \qquad |H(f)|^2 \text{ a Butterworth band-pass at } f_0 \text{ with quality } Q = f_0/\Delta f
card.simulation: Second-order Butterworth band-pass; center \(f_0\) log-uniform on [0.05, 0.4] cycles/sample (at least 50 cycles per record), \(Q\) log-uniform on [2, 30].
references: Oppenheim & Schafer (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed. Pearson.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(h\): the filter's impulse response; \(*\): convolution; \(H(f)\): its frequency response
\(f_0\): the center frequency (cycles per sample); \(\Delta f\): the bandwidth; \(Q = f_0/\Delta f\): the quality factor

card.description: Gaussian noise through a low-pass or a high-pass Butterworth filter.
card.simulation: Low-pass for even instances, high-pass for odd; cutoff \(f_c\) log-uniform on [0.02, 0.4] cycles/sample, order \(n \in \{2, \dots, 8\}\).
references: Oppenheim & Schafer (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed. Pearson.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(h\): the filter's impulse response; \(*\): convolution; \(H(f)\): its frequency response
\(f_c\): the cutoff frequency; \(n\): the filter order; the exponent is \(+2n\) for low-pass and \(-2n\) for high-pass

card.description: A Gaussian process with a spectrum nobody named. Its log power spectrum is itself a smooth random function of log-frequency.
references: Percival & Walden (1993). Spectral Analysis for Physical Applications. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(S(f)\): the power spectrum; \(f_k\): the Fourier frequencies
\(\varphi_k\): independent uniform random phases
\(\mathrm{GP}\): a smooth Gaussian process in \(\log f\)

classes.name: Linear non-Gaussian
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M24 8 C27 12 37 13 44 20 C39 26 30 27 24 32 C18 27 9 26 4 20 C11 13 21 12 24 8 Z"/><path d="M24 32 C24 37 28 38 30 41 C32 44 35 44 37 43"/><circle cx="20" cy="18" r="1.5" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="28" cy="18" r="1.5" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></svg>
classes.motto: The stingray glides in a straight line, trailing a long, heavy tail.
classes.title: linear non-Gaussian
classes.blurb: Linear filters driven by skewed, heavy-tailed or bounded innovations.

card.description: Linear autoregressions driven by skewed (centered gamma) innovations. The dependence is linear, but the marginal and the dynamics are asymmetric.
card.simulation: \(p \le 3\); shape \(k\) log-uniform on [0.4, 3], so innovation skewness \(2/\sqrt{k}\) runs from about 1.2 to 3.2.
references: Lawrance (1991). Directionality and reversibility in time series. Int. Stat. Rev. 59, 67–79.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\phi_k\): autoregressive coefficients (order \(p\))
\(\varepsilon_t\): centered gamma innovations; \(g_t\): a gamma draw with shape \(k\)

card.description: Autoregressions driven by heavy-tailed Student-t innovations, so large shocks propagate through the linear filter.
card.simulation: Order \(p \in \{1, 2, 3\}\) with stable coefficients from reflection coefficients; Student-t \(\nu\) stratified over [3, 6] in this profile (finite variance; the full profile also has α-stable innovations).
references: Box, Jenkins, Reinsel & Ljung (2015). Time Series Analysis, 5th ed. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\phi_k\): the autoregressive coefficients (order \(p\))
\(\varepsilon_t\): Student-t innovations with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom

card.description: A one-sided, decaying moving average of skewed innovations. A linear process can be time-irreversible when its innovations are non-Gaussian and its filter is asymmetric (Weiss 1975).
references: Weiss (1975). Time-reversibility of linear stochastic processes. J. Appl. Probab. 12, 831–836.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\theta_j\): the moving-average coefficients, decaying with lag (order \(q\))
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent skewed innovations

fixed: Jump sizes \(Y_k \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\)
card.description: An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-type process driven by compound-Poisson jumps (a Lévy-driven OU): each jump kicks the state, which then decays exponentially. The paths are sawtooth-like and time-irreversible.
equations: x_t = a\, x_{t-1} + J_t + \sigma \eta_t, \qquad J_t = \textstyle\sum_{\text{jumps in } t} Y_k,\ \ Y_k \sim \mathrm{Exp}
card.simulation: Jump rate log-uniform on [0.05, 0.4] per sample, exponential jump sizes (one-sided for even instances, two-sided for odd), decay \(a\) stratified over [0.6, 0.93] (decay times of about 2.5–14 samples). Instances 0, 1, 4, 5, … add a Gaussian part with \(\sigma = 0.3\).
references: Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard (2001). Non-Gaussian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-based models and some of their uses in financial economics. J. R. Stat. Soc. B 63, 167–241.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(a\): the decay factor per sample
\(J_t\): the sum of the jumps arriving in sample \(t\) (Poisson arrivals); \(Y_k\): exponential jump sizes
\(\eta_t\): Gaussian noise with scale \(\sigma\) (zero for the pure jump process)

card.description: An AR(1) driven by bounded innovations (binary ±1 or uniform). For binary input and \(|\phi| \le 1/2\) the stationary law is a Cantor-like or uniform measure rather than a Gaussian.
card.simulation: \(\phi\) stratified over (−0.9, 0.9); binary innovations for even instances, uniform for odd.
references: Solomyak (1995). On the random series Σ ±λ^n (an Erdős problem). Ann. Math. 142, 611–625.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\phi\): the autoregressive coefficient
\(\varepsilon_t\): binary \(\pm 1\) or uniform innovations

fixed: Pulse amplitudes \(A_k \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)\)
card.description: Poisson shot noise, a superposition of identical pulses arriving at random times. It is linear (a filtered point process) and non-Gaussian.
card.simulation: Pulse shape \(h\) exponential, alpha-function or Gaussian; rate \(\lambda\) log-uniform on [0.05, 0.3] per sample; width log-uniform on [1.5, 6] samples; exponential amplitudes \(A_k\).
references: Rice (1944). Mathematical analysis of random noise. Bell Syst. Tech. J. 23, 282–332.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_k\): pulse arrival times, a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) per sample
\(A_k\): the pulse amplitudes; \(h\): the pulse shape

classes.name: Long memory
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M20 14 C28 11 40 14 41 25 L41 37 M36 37 L36 30 M26 30 L26 37 M20 37 L20 29"/><path d="M20 14 C13 12 8 16 8 22 C8 26 9 30 7 34 C6 37 9 39 11 37"/><path d="M18 16 C24 16 26 22 24 28 C21 29 17 27 16 24"/><path d="M20 29 C24 31 34 31 41 29"/><circle cx="12.5" cy="19" r="1.5" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/></svg>
classes.title: long memory, self-similar, multifractal
classes.blurb: Power-law correlations, fractional processes and multiplicative cascades.

card.description: Fractional Gaussian noise, the increments of fractional Brownian motion: stationary and Gaussian, with power-law autocorrelation. \(H > 1/2\) gives long memory (persistence), \(H < 1/2\) anti-persistence.
card.simulation: Exact circulant-embedding synthesis (Davies–Harte); \(H\) stratified over [0.02, 0.9].
references: Mandelbrot & Van Ness (1968). Fractional Brownian motions, fractional noises and applications. SIAM Rev. 10, 422–437.
Davies & Harte (1987). Tests for Hurst effect. Biometrika 74, 95–101.
where: \(\gamma(k)\): the autocovariance at lag \(k\)
\(\sigma^2\): the variance; \(H\): the Hurst exponent

card.description: Fractionally integrated ARMA: a fractional difference operator gives hyperbolically decaying autocorrelation, with short-memory ARMA structure on top.
card.simulation: \(d\) stratified over [−0.45, 0.4] (stationary and invertible); \(p, q \in \{0, 1\}\) with coefficients uniform on [−0.6, 0.6].
references: Granger & Joyeux (1980). An introduction to long-memory time series models and fractional differencing. J. Time Ser. Anal. 1, 15–29.
Hosking (1981). Fractional differencing. Biometrika 68, 165–176.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(B\): the backshift operator, \(B x_t = x_{t-1}\)
\(\phi(B), \theta(B)\): the AR and MA polynomials
\(d\): the fractional differencing order; \(\binom{d}{k}\): the generalized binomial coefficient

card.description: Increments of the multifractal random walk: a noise modulated by a log-correlated (multifractal) volatility, giving intermittent bursts at every scale and scale-dependent heavy tails.
card.simulation: \(\epsilon_t\) fractional Gaussian noise with \(H\) stratified over [0.3, 0.7] (Student-t innovations for odd instances); intermittency \(\lambda^2\) over [0.03, 0.15]; integral scale \(L\) log-uniform on [64, 1024]. Generated at length 8192 and windowed.
references: Bacry, Delour & Muzy (2001). Multifractal random walk. Phys. Rev. E 64, 026103.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\epsilon_t\): fractional Gaussian noise with Hurst exponent \(H\)
\(\omega_t\): the log-volatility, a log-correlated Gaussian process
\(\lambda^2\): the intermittency coefficient; \(L\): the integral scale (in samples)

card.description: A noise modulated by a multiplicative cascade on a dyadic tree: the binomial p-model or a log-Poisson cascade. Volatility is intermittent in a scale-invariant way.
card.simulation: p-model with \(p\) stratified over [0.55, 0.68] (even instances), log-Poisson cascade (odd); random grid phase.
references: Meneveau & Sreenivasan (1987). Simple multifractal cascade model for fully developed turbulence. Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 1424.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\epsilon_t\): fractional Gaussian noise
\(W_{j, k}\): the random weight of box \(k\) at cascade level \(j\); \(k_j(t)\): the box containing \(t\); \(J\): the number of levels
\(p\): the p-model's weight parameter

card.description: Long-memory stochastic volatility, in which the log-volatility is itself a persistent fractional Gaussian noise.
card.simulation: \(\eta\) fGn with \(H_w\) stratified over [0.75, 0.95]; scale \(s\) over [0.3, 0.8].
references: Breidt, Crato & de Lima (1998). The detection and estimation of long memory in stochastic volatility. J. Econometrics 83, 325–348.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\epsilon^{(H)}_t\): fractional Gaussian noise with Hurst exponent \(H\)
\(\eta^{(H_w)}_t\): a second, persistent fGn with Hurst exponent \(H_w\), driving the log-volatility
\(s\): the volatility scale

card.description: Power-law (1/f) noise with exponent below 1, where the process is still stationary.
card.simulation: Spectral synthesis (random phases on a power-law amplitude spectrum); \(\beta\) stratified over [0, 0.95].
references: Keshner (1982). 1/f noise. Proc. IEEE 70, 212–218.
where: \(S(f)\): the power spectrum at frequency \(f\)
\(\beta\): the spectral exponent

classes.name: Nonlinear stochastic
classes.motto: The chameleon changes with its surroundings: new conditions, new regime.
classes.title: nonlinear stochastic, discrete time
classes.blurb: Thresholds, volatility clustering, hidden regimes and random coefficients.

card.description: Self-exciting threshold autoregression: the AR coefficient switches when a lagged value of the series itself crosses a threshold, giving piecewise-linear dynamics with asymmetric cycles.
card.simulation: 2 regimes (threshold 0) or 3 (two thresholds uniform on [−1, 1]); delay \(d \in \{1, 2, 3\}\); regime coefficients \(\phi\) stratified over [0.4, 0.9], uniform on [−0.6, 0.2] and (third regime) on [−0.3, 0.7].
references: Tong & Lim (1980). Threshold autoregression, limit cycles and cyclical data. J. R. Stat. Soc. B 42, 245–292.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(j\): the regime; \(\phi^{(j)}\): its autoregressive coefficient
\(r_j\): the regime thresholds; \(d\): the delay of the switching variable

card.description: Exponential autoregression: the AR coefficient depends smoothly on the previous value, so small and large excursions relax at different rates. It can support limit cycles.
references: Haggan & Ozaki (1981). Modelling nonlinear random vibrations using an amplitude-dependent autoregressive time series model. Biometrika 68, 189–196.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(a, b\): the coefficients of the amplitude-dependent AR coefficient

card.description: A bilinear moving average. The autocorrelation is zero beyond lag 0, like white noise, but the series is not independent; the dependence shows up in higher-order moments.
card.simulation: \(c\) stratified over [0.4, 1]; Gaussian innovations (even instances) or skewed (odd).
references: Granger & Andersen (1978). An Introduction to Bilinear Time Series Models. Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(c\): the bilinear coefficient

card.description: An AR(1) whose coefficient is redrawn at every step, giving conditional heteroskedasticity and heavy tails from a linear-looking recursion.
card.simulation: \(\sigma_\phi\) stratified over [0.1, 0.4].
references: Nicholls & Quinn (1982). Random Coefficient Autoregressive Models. Springer.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(\phi\): the mean AR coefficient; \(\sigma_\phi\): its standard deviation
\(\eta_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise, redrawn each sample

card.description: Conditionally heteroskedastic returns: volatility clusters because today's variance depends on yesterday's squared shock. GJR and EGARCH variants add the leverage effect (asymmetry in the sign of the shock).
card.simulation: ARCH(1), GARCH(1,1), GJR-GARCH or EGARCH with Gaussian or Student-t \(z_t\); persistence stratified over [0.6, 0.99].
references: Engle (1982). Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity with estimates of the variance of United Kingdom inflation. Econometrica 50, 987–1007.
Bollerslev (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. J. Econometrics 31, 307–327.
where: \(r_t\): the observed returns
\(\sigma_t^2\): the conditional variance; \(z_t\): independent Gaussian or Student-t shocks
\(\omega, \alpha, \beta\): the GARCH coefficients; \(\gamma\): the leverage (asymmetry) coefficient
\(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\): the indicator function; \(\mathbb{E}|z|\): the mean absolute shock

card.description: Stochastic volatility, in which the log-variance follows its own autoregression driven by a separate noise.
card.simulation: \(\phi\) stratified over [0.8, 0.95], \(\sigma\) over [0.15, 0.4].
references: Taylor (1986). Modelling Financial Time Series. Wiley.
where: \(r_t\): the observed returns
\(h_t\): the log-variance; \(\phi\): its persistence; \(\sigma\): its noise scale
\(z_t, \eta_t\): independent standard Gaussian noises

card.description: An AR(1) whose parameters switch between regimes according to a hidden Markov chain.
card.simulation: 2–4 regimes with mean dwell log-uniform on [8, 60] samples (at least about 15 regime changes per record); regimes differ in a drawn subset of \(\{\phi, \mu, \sigma\}\).
references: Hamilton (1989). A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series and the business cycle. Econometrica 57, 357–384.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(s_t\): the hidden regime, a Markov chain
\(\mu_s, \phi_s, \sigma_s\): the mean, AR coefficient and noise scale of regime \(s\)

card.description: Hidden Markov models: a discrete hidden chain read out through noisy Gaussian emissions. The cyclic three-state chain violates detailed balance, so the series is time-irreversible.
card.simulation: Two-state (even instances) or cyclic three-state (odd) chains with Gaussian emissions; mean dwell log-uniform on [4, 50] samples.
references: Rabiner (1989). A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proc. IEEE 77, 257–286.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(s_t\): the hidden state, a Markov chain with transition probabilities \(P(s_t \mid s_{t-1})\)
\(\mu_s, \sigma_s\): the emission mean and standard deviation of state \(s\)

card.description: Chaotic maps with dynamical noise added at every step, so the orbit is perturbed as it evolves rather than only when it is measured.
equations: x_{n+1} = f_\mu(x_n) + \sigma \eta_n, \qquad f \in \{\text{logistic, tent, Hénon, Ricker, Holmes}\}
card.simulation: Noise level log-stratified over [0.01, 0.1] (weaker noise left the orbit indistinguishable from the clean map), scaled to each map (additive for logistic, tent and Hénon; for Ricker it enters the exponent, as environmental noise). Map parameters are redrawn until the noise-free map is chaotic. One instance is the Holmes (Duffing) map \(x \mapsto y,\ y \mapsto -0.2x + 2.7y - y^3\), a map with no clean twin in the collection.
references: Crutchfield, Farmer & Huberman (1982). Fluctuations and simple chaotic dynamics. Phys. Rep. 92, 45–82.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(f_\mu\): the deterministic map with parameter \(\mu\)
\(\sigma\): the dynamical noise scale; \(\eta_n\): independent standard Gaussian noise

card.description: Smooth-transition autoregressions: the AR coefficients move smoothly between two regimes as a lagged value crosses a threshold (logistic or exponential transition), plus additive nonlinear ARs.
equations: G_{\mathrm{L}} = \left[1 + e^{-\gamma x_{t-1}}\right]^{-1}, \qquad G_{\mathrm{E}} = 1 - e^{-\gamma x_{t-1}^2/4}
card.simulation: LSTAR, ESTAR, or additive \(x_t = g(x_{t-1}) + \varepsilon_t\) with \(g\) a sine or tanh; steepness \(\gamma\) log-uniform on [1, 20]; \(\phi_1\) uniform on [0.2, 0.8], \(\phi_2\) on [−0.8, 0.2].
references: Teräsvirta (1994). Specification, estimation, and evaluation of smooth transition autoregressive models. J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 89, 208–218.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(\phi_1, \phi_2\): the AR coefficients in the two regimes
\(G\): the transition function (logistic \(G_{\mathrm{L}}\) or exponential \(G_{\mathrm{E}}\)), centered at 0; \(\gamma\): its steepness

card.description: A second-order Volterra series, a moving average with quadratic cross terms between lagged innovations.
card.simulation: Nonlinear weight \(w\) stratified over [0.3, 1].
references: Schetzen (1980). The Volterra and Wiener Theories of Nonlinear Systems. Wiley.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(h_j\): the linear kernel; \(h_{jk}\): the quadratic kernel; \(w\): the weight of the quadratic part

fixed: Step size \(h = 0.1\)
card.description: A noisy double-well map. The state lingers near one of two stable points and hops between them at noise-driven, irregular times.
card.simulation: \(h = 0.1\); \(\sigma\) stratified over [0.22, 0.4], so there are at least about 40 well crossings per record.
references: Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(h\): the step size; \(\sigma\): the noise scale

card.description: Noise-induced switching between two chaotic attractors. Just below its attractor-merging crisis, the symmetric cubic map has two mirror-image chaotic bands; weak noise kicks the orbit between them.
card.simulation: \(a\) stratified over [2.50, 2.58]; noise \(\sigma\) log-uniform on [0.03, 0.06].
references: Grebogi, Ott & Yorke (1983). Crises, sudden changes in chaotic attractors, and transient chaos. Physica D 7, 181–200.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(a\): the map parameter; \(\sigma\): the noise scale; \(\eta_n\): independent standard Gaussian noise

card.description: A Kesten random multiplicative process. Occasional runs of multipliers above 1 give bursts of exponential growth, and the stationary law has a power-law tail even though the inputs are light-tailed.
equations: x_{n+1} = a_n x_n + b_n, \qquad \ln a_n \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2),\ m < 0
card.simulation: Tail exponent \(\kappa\) stratified over [2.3, 4] (finite variance).
references: Kesten (1973). Random difference equations and renewal theory for products of random matrices. Acta Math. 131, 207–248.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(a_n\): random multipliers, log-normal with log-mean \(m\) and log-standard deviation \(s\)
\(b_n\): positive random additive terms
\(\kappa\): the exponent of the power-law tail

classes.name: Deterministic maps
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M8 31 C8 21 15 19 24 19 C33 19 40 21 40 31 C40 36 33 38 24 38 C15 38 8 36 8 31 Z"/><circle cx="16" cy="16" r="5"/><circle cx="32" cy="16" r="5"/><circle cx="16" cy="16" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="32" cy="16" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M16 30 Q24 34 32 30"/></svg>
classes.motto: The frog travels in discrete hops, one iterate at a time.
classes.title: deterministic maps
classes.blurb: Iterated maps, from the logistic map to strange nonchaotic attractors.

card.description: The logistic map across its chaotic range, beyond the period-doubling cascade. Parameters that land in a periodic window are redrawn, so every instance is chaotic.
card.simulation: \(r\) stratified over [3.5, 4] and redrawn on [3.57, 4] until the Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda\), estimated along the orbit, is positive; burn-in discarded.
references: May (1976). Simple mathematical models with very complicated dynamics. Nature 261, 459–467.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(r\): the growth parameter

card.description: Classic one-dimensional chaotic maps across their chaotic ranges.
equations: \text{cubic: } x \mapsto a x (1 - x^2), \qquad \text{Chebyshev: } x \mapsto \cos(k \arccos x)
references: Collet & Eckmann (1980). Iterated Maps on the Interval as Dynamical Systems. Birkhäuser.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(\mu\), \(a\): the map parameters; \(k\): the Chebyshev order

card.description: The sine circle map above its critical coupling \(K = 1\), where the map is no longer invertible and chaos appears between the overlapping mode-locked (Arnold tongue) regions.
card.simulation: \(K\) stratified over [1.05, 2.5], \(\Omega\) uniform on [0.05, 0.95]; periodic orbits are redrawn; observed through \(\sin 2\pi\theta\) to remove the wrap.
references: Jensen, Bak & Bohr (1984). Transition to chaos by interaction of resonances in dissipative systems. I. Circle maps. Phys. Rev. A 30, 1960–1969.
where: \(\theta_n\): the phase at iteration \(n\), in \([0, 1)\); \(x_n\): the observed series
\(\Omega\): the bare frequency (winding); \(K\): the nonlinearity (coupling) strength

card.description: Type-I intermittency: long laminar phases creeping away from a marginally stable fixed point at 0, interrupted by chaotic bursts that reinject the orbit near 0.
card.simulation: \(z\) stratified over [1.3, 1.85], where the invariant measure is finite (\(z \to 2\) is the infinite-measure boundary); laminar phases of tens of samples, many per record.
references: Pomeau & Manneville (1980). Intermittent transition to turbulence in dissipative dynamical systems. Commun. Math. Phys. 74, 189–197.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(z\): the order of tangency at the marginal fixed point \(x = 0\)

card.description: The Bernoulli (doubling) shift, the textbook fully chaotic map, and the Gauss map, which generates continued-fraction digits.
card.simulation: The doubling map is iterated in exact rational arithmetic, because floating point collapses it to 0 within about 53 steps.
references: Lasota & Mackey (1994). Chaos, Fractals, and Noise, 2nd ed. Springer.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration

card.description: Piecewise maps with a square-root branch, the normal form near a grazing impact (Nordmark map). The square-root singularity gives strong stretching on one side of the border.
equations: x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} a x_n + d & x_n < 0 \\ -c\sqrt{x_n} + d & x_n \ge 0 \end{cases}
card.simulation: \(a\) stratified over [0.5, 0.95]; \(c\) uniform on [1, 3] and \(d\) on [0.2, 0.8], redrawn until the Lyapunov exponent is positive. The map is continuous at the border \(x = 0\).
references: Nordmark (1991). Non-periodic motion caused by grazing incidence in an impact oscillator. J. Sound Vib. 145, 279–297.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(a\): the slope of the linear branch; \(c\): the square-root coefficient; \(d\): the common offset (the value at the border)

card.description: One trajectory from each of 18 usable discrete-time maps in the dysts database, observed in one coordinate.
card.simulation: Default dysts parameters, a perturbed initial condition, burn-in discarded. Circle, Duffing and Gingerbreadman are excluded (unbounded, drifting or periodic at their defaults); a near-regular coordinate is swapped for the map's other coordinate.
references: Gilpin (2021). Chaos as an interpretable benchmark for forecasting and data-driven modelling. NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks.
where: \(\mathbf{u}_n\): the map's state at iteration \(n\); \(\mathbf{F}\): its update rule (explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(u_{c,n}\): the observed coordinate \(c\)

card.description: Regime sweeps of two-dimensional maps: Hénon, Lozi, Ikeda, the Chirikov standard map from mixed KAM tori and chaos to global chaos, Arnold's cat, Burgers and a coupled logistic pair.
equations: \text{Hénon: } x_{n+1} = 1 - a x_n^2 + y_n,\ \ y_{n+1} = b x_n
card.simulation: One parameter swept per map; \(a\) for Hénon (periodic windows redrawn) and Lozi, \(u\) on [0.7, 0.9] for Ikeda, and \(K \in \{0.5, 2.5, 3, 4.5, 6\}\) for the standard map, observed as \(\sin\theta\).
references: Hénon (1976). A two-dimensional mapping with a strange attractor. Commun. Math. Phys. 50, 69–77.
Chirikov (1979). A universal instability of many-dimensional oscillator systems. Phys. Rep. 52, 263–379.
where: \(x_n, y_n\): the Hénon map's coordinates; \(a, b\): its parameters
\(\theta_n, p_n\): the standard map's angle and momentum; \(K\): the kick strength

card.description: Deterministic but aperiodic real-valued sequences: the density of live cells in successive rows of an elementary cellular automaton, rule 30 (Wolfram class 3, chaotic) and rule 110 (class 4, a periodic background crossed by interacting gliders).
card.simulation: Rule 30 on 3000 cells and rule 110 on 8000 cells, from random initial rows; the transient is discarded.
references: Wolfram (1983). Statistical mechanics of cellular automata. Rev. Mod. Phys. 55, 601–644.
where: \(s_i^{(n)} \in \{0, 1\}\): cell \(i\) in row \(n\) of the automaton; \(\oplus\): exclusive or; \(\lor\): or (the rule-30 update shown; rule 110 has its own lookup table)
\(W\): the row width; \(x_n\): the fraction of live cells in row \(n\)

card.description: The Rulkov map neuron: a fast variable that spikes chaotically and a slow variable that switches bursting on and off, giving bursts of spikes separated by silent recovery.
card.simulation: \(\alpha\) stratified over [4.1, 4.6]; \(\mu\) log-uniform on [0.003, 0.01] sets the burst period (about 10 bursts per record).
references: Rulkov (2001). Regularization of synchronized chaotic bursts. Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 183–186.
where: \(x_n\): the fast (membrane-potential-like) variable, observed; \(y_n\): the slow recovery variable
\(\alpha\): the nonlinearity; \(\mu\): the slow time-scale ratio; \(\sigma\): the slow variable's set point

card.description: A strange nonchaotic attractor: quasi-periodic forcing makes the attractor fractal, yet its Lyapunov exponent is negative, so it is strange without being chaotic.
card.simulation: \(\omega\) the golden mean, \(\sigma > 1\).
references: Grebogi, Ott, Pelikan & Yorke (1984). Strange attractors that are not chaotic. Physica D 13, 261–268.
where: \(x_n\): the observed state
\(\theta_n\): the quasi-periodic forcing phase; \(\omega\): its frequency (the golden mean)
\(\sigma\): the forcing strength

classes.name: Chaotic flows
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M24 22 C18 10 6 9 6 17 C6 24 16 26 24 22 Z"/><path d="M24 22 C30 10 42 9 42 17 C42 24 32 26 24 22 Z"/><path d="M24 24 C19 28 12 36 17 39 C21 41 24 34 24 24 Z"/><path d="M24 24 C29 28 36 36 31 39 C27 41 24 34 24 24 Z"/><path d="M24 14 V38 M24 14 L20 7 M24 14 L28 7"/></svg>
classes.motto: One flap of a butterfly's wings, and the future is a different place.
classes.title: chaotic flows
classes.blurb: Strange attractors of ordinary and delay differential equations.

card.description: One trajectory from each usable chaotic flow in the dysts database, from Lorenz and Rössler to lesser-known systems of chemistry, circuits and fluid mechanics. Each instance names its system.
card.simulation: DOP853, resampled to 15–40 points per period and coarsened where the autocorrelation time exceeds 5 samples; a random coordinate \(c\), perturbed initial condition, burn-in discarded, optional measurement noise \(\eta_t\). \(\lambda_{\max}\) from a Benettin estimate, per sample.
references: Gilpin (2021). Chaos as an interpretable benchmark for forecasting and data-driven modelling. NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks.
where: \(\mathbf{u}\): the system's state vector; \(\mathbf{f}\): its vector field (its explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(u_c\): the observed coordinate \(c\) of the state
\(\Delta t\): the sampling interval, \(T/n_p\), with \(T\) the system's dominant period in its own time units
\(t_0\): the time at the end of the discarded transient (burn-in)
\(n_p\): the number of samples per period of the system's dominant oscillation (points per period)
\(\eta_t\): white measurement noise added to the observation

card.description: Regimes of canonical chaotic flows that the dysts defaults miss: Lorenz at ρ = 24.5 (chaos coexisting with stable fixed points) and at ρ = 130 (far above the classic ρ = 28), the Chen system, the Rössler funnel (a = 0.3, c = 14), Chua's double scroll, the forced Duffing oscillator, the driven damped pendulum, the double pendulum and Lorenz-84.
equations: \text{Lorenz: } \dot x = \sigma(y - x),\ \ \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y,\ \ \dot z = xy - \beta z
\text{Rössler: } \dot x = -y - z,\ \ \dot y = x + a y,\ \ \dot z = b + z(x - c)
references: Lorenz (1963). Deterministic nonperiodic flow. J. Atmos. Sci. 20, 130–141.
Rössler (1976). An equation for continuous chaos. Phys. Lett. A 57, 397–398.
where: \(x, y, z\): the state variables; the dot is the time derivative
Lorenz: \(\sigma, \rho, \beta\); Rössler: \(a, b, c\)
Duffing: \(\delta\) damping, \(\gamma\) forcing amplitude, \(\omega\) forcing frequency
Each series' explicit equations and observed variable are shown with it

card.description: Chaotic delay-differential equations, whose infinite-dimensional state gives high-dimensional chaos from a single scalar feedback loop: Mackey–Glass, the Ikeda delay equation, Uçar's cubic prototype (slow, wandering chaos) and the band-pass optoelectronic Ikeda oscillator (chaotic switching between plateaus).
equations: \text{Mackey–Glass: } \dot x = \beta \frac{x_\tau}{1 + x_\tau^{n}} - \gamma x, \qquad \text{Ikeda: } \dot x = -x + \mu \sin(x_\tau), \qquad x_\tau = x(t - \tau)
\text{Uçar: } \dot x = x_\tau - x_\tau^3, \qquad \text{band-pass Ikeda: } \epsilon \dot x = -x - y/\theta + \beta \sin^2(x_\tau + \phi),\ \ \dot y = x
card.simulation: Mackey–Glass with \(\beta = 0.2, \gamma = 0.1, n = 10\) and \(\tau\) stratified over [17, 40] (the chaotic range); Ikeda with \(\tau = 2\), \(\mu\) stratified over [5, 30]; Uçar with \(\tau\) over [1.6, 1.7]; these by fixed-step RK4 on an integer delay grid, resampled to 15–40 points per period. Band-pass Ikeda with \(\tau = 1\), \(\epsilon = 0.01\), \(\theta = 50\), \(\phi = -\pi/4\) and \(\beta\) over [2, 2.5], observed every 0.02 (20 delays per record).
references: Mackey & Glass (1977). Oscillation and chaos in physiological control systems. Science 197, 287–289.
Ikeda & Matsumoto (1987). High-dimensional chaotic behavior in systems with time-delayed feedback. Physica D 29, 223–235.
Uçar (2002). A prototype model for chaos studies. Int. J. Eng. Sci. 40, 251–258.
Peil, Jacquot, Chembo, Larger & Erneux (2009). Routes to chaos and multiple time scale dynamics in broadband bandpass nonlinear delay electro-optic oscillators. Phys. Rev. E 79, 026208.
where: \(x\): the state (observed); \(x_\tau = x(t - \tau)\): its value a delay \(\tau\) ago
Mackey–Glass: \(\beta\) production, \(\gamma\) decay, \(n\) nonlinearity; Ikeda: \(\mu\) feedback gain
Band-pass Ikeda: \(y\) the integrated (low-frequency) variable, \(\epsilon\) and \(\theta\) the fast and slow filter time scales, \(\beta\) the feedback gain, \(\phi\) the operating-point offset

card.description: Chaotic dysts flows sampled coarsely, at 4–10 points per period (80–250 periods per record), the regime of Empirical1000's own chaotic-flow series.
references: Gilpin (2021). Chaos as an interpretable benchmark for forecasting and data-driven modelling. NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks.
where: \(\mathbf{u}\): the system's state vector; \(\mathbf{f}\): its vector field (its explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(u_c\): the observed coordinate \(c\) of the state
\(\Delta t\): the sampling interval, \(T/n_p\), with \(T\) the system's dominant period in its own time units
\(n_p\): the number of samples per period of the system's dominant oscillation (points per period)
\(\eta_t\): white measurement noise added to the observation

card.description: A second realization of six systems whose single dysts-flow instance was the most interesting: Sakarya, ZhouChen, BlinkingRotlet, Halvorsen, Rabinovich–Fabrikant and Dadras. Each uses a different observed coordinate, sampling density and initial condition.
references: Gilpin (2021). Chaos as an interpretable benchmark for forecasting and data-driven modelling. NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks.
where: \(\mathbf{u}\): the system's state vector; \(\mathbf{f}\): its vector field (its explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(u_c\): the observed coordinate \(c\) of the state
\(\Delta t\): the sampling interval, \(T/n_p\), with \(T\) the system's dominant period in its own time units
\(n_p\): the number of samples per period of the system's dominant oscillation (points per period)
\(\eta_t\): white measurement noise added to the observation

card.description: Chaotic advection: a tracer in a Stokes flow stirred by two rotlets that switch on and off alternately. Each flow alone is integrable; switching between them creates chaos.
card.simulation: Switching period \(\tau\) log-uniform on [0.8, 10]; short periods give fast irregular mixing, long ones smooth rotation broken by bursts at each switch. Observed x or y.
references: Meleshko & Aref (1996). A blinking rotlet model for chaotic advection. Phys. Fluids 8, 3215–3217.
where: \(\mathbf{r}\): the tracer's position
\(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\): the velocity fields of the two rotlets
\(\tau\): the switching period; \(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\): the indicator function

card.description: The Bunimovich stadium billiard, Hamiltonian chaos made of straight flights and specular bounces off the walls.
card.simulation: Half-length \(L\) stratified over [0.5, 2]; x or y sampled at fixed time steps, about three samples per flight.
references: Bunimovich (1979). On the ergodic properties of nowhere dispersing billiards. Commun. Math. Phys. 65, 295–312.
where: \(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}\): the particle's position and velocity
\(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\): the unit normal to the wall at the point of impact

card.description: A ball bouncing on a sinusoidally vibrating table: ballistic flights under gravity joined by inelastic impacts. It is chaotic for moderate table accelerations.
equations: \ddot{z} = -g \ \ \text{between impacts}, \qquad \dot z^{+} - \dot s = -e\,(\dot z^{-} - \dot s), \quad s(t) = A\sin\omega t
card.simulation: Normalized acceleration \(\Gamma = A\omega^2/g\) in about [2.5, 4], restitution \(e\) drawn; ball height sampled 6 times per table period.
references: Holmes (1982). The dynamics of repeated impacts with a sinusoidally vibrating table. J. Sound Vib. 84, 173–189.
where: \(z\): the ball's height; \(s(t)\): the table's height
\(g\): gravitational acceleration; \(e\): the coefficient of restitution
\(A, \omega\): the table's amplitude and angular frequency; \(\pm\): just after/before an impact

classes.name: Oscillators
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="24" cy="36" r="10" stroke-opacity=".28" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse cx="24" cy="36" rx="4.5" ry="5.5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".4"/><path d="M24 14 C17 14 15 21 16 30.5 L24 30.5 Z M24 14 C31 14 33 21 32 30.5 L24 30.5 Z"/><circle cx="24" cy="10.5" r="3.2"/><path d="M22.5 8 L19 3.5 M25.5 8 L29 3.5"/><path d="M16.5 19.5 L11.5 17.5 M16 25 L11 26.5 M31.5 19.5 L36.5 17.5 M32 25 L37 26.5"/></svg>
classes.motto: Fireflies flash in rhythm, and whole trees of them fall into step.
classes.title: periodic, quasi-periodic, oscillatory
classes.blurb: Limit cycles, tori and shaped oscillations.

card.description: A pure sinusoid, from near the Nyquist frequency to very slow.
card.simulation: Period \(P\) log-uniform on [2.2, 60] samples (at least 16 cycles per record).
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(P\): the period in samples; \(\varphi\): the phase

card.description: Periodic waveforms made of many harmonics, a sawtooth or a random set of harmonics.
card.simulation: Sawtooth, or \(K \in \{2, \dots, 20\}\) harmonics with random, decaying amplitudes and random phases; period \(P\) log-uniform on [8, 120] samples.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(K\): the number of harmonics; \(a_k, \varphi_k\): their amplitudes and phases; \(P\): the fundamental period

card.description: Motion on a 2- or 3-torus, a sum of sinusoids with incommensurate frequencies. It never exactly repeats.
equations: x_t = \sum_{k=1}^{2\text{ or }3} a_k \sin(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k), \qquad f_i/f_j \notin \mathbb{Q}
card.simulation: Frequency ratios near the golden mean and \(\sqrt 2\); random amplitudes.
references: Pikovsky, Rosenblum & Kurths (2001). Synchronization: A Universal Concept in Nonlinear Sciences. Cambridge University Press.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(f_k\): incommensurate frequencies (ratios not rational); \(a_k, \varphi_k\): amplitudes and phases
\(\mathbb{Q}\): the rational numbers

fixed: Stuart–Landau: \(\omega = 1\); FitzHugh–Nagumo: \(a = 0.7\), \(b = 0.8\), \(\varepsilon = 0.08\)
card.description: Self-sustained oscillators on a stable limit cycle, from nearly sinusoidal to relaxation oscillations.
equations: \text{van der Pol: } \ddot x - \mu (1 - x^2)\dot x + x = 0
\text{Brusselator: } \dot x = a + x^2 y - (b + 1) x,\ \ \dot y = b x - x^2 y
\text{FitzHugh–Nagumo: } \dot v = v - v^3/3 - w + I,\ \ \dot w = \epsilon\,(v + a - b w)
card.simulation: van der Pol (\(\mu\) log-stratified over [0.1, 10]; two instances), the Brusselator (\(b > 1 + a^2\)) and oscillatory FitzHugh–Nagumo (\(I\) uniform on [0.5, 1.2]; two instances), integrated and resampled to 15–40 points per period.
references: van der Pol (1926). On relaxation-oscillations. Phil. Mag. 2, 978–992.
where: \(x\): the observed variable; \(\mu\): the van der Pol nonlinearity
Brusselator: \(x, y\) the intermediate concentrations, \(a, b\) the feed parameters
FitzHugh–Nagumo: \(v\) the fast variable, \(w\) the recovery variable, \(I\) the input, \(a, b, \epsilon\) the recovery parameters

card.description: Amplitude-modulated, frequency-modulated and beating oscillations with stationary modulation.
equations: \text{AM: } (1 + m\cos 2\pi f_m t) \cos 2\pi f_c t, \qquad \text{FM: } \cos\!\left(2\pi f_c t + \beta \sin 2\pi f_m t\right)
where: \(f_c\): the carrier frequency; \(f_m\): the modulation frequency
\(m\): the AM modulation depth; \(\beta\): the FM modulation index

card.description: Periodic orbits of flows that are chaotic at other parameters, Rössler at c = 8.5 (period 4, in its period-doubling cascade) and Lorenz at ρ = 350 (a periodic window).
equations: \text{Rössler: } \dot x = -y - z,\ \ \dot y = x + a y,\ \ \dot z = b + z(x - c)
references: Rössler (1976). An equation for continuous chaos. Phys. Lett. A 57, 397–398.
Sparrow (1982). The Lorenz Equations: Bifurcations, Chaos, and Strange Attractors. Springer.
where: \(x, y, z\): the Rössler state; \(a, b, c\): its parameters (explicit values are shown with each series)

card.description: Periodic orbits with unusual waveforms: Hindmarsh–Rose periodic bursting, the triangle-like Rayleigh oscillator, a conservative Lotka–Volterra orbit far from equilibrium (sharp pulses on a flat floor) and a pendulum librating just inside its separatrix.
references: Hindmarsh & Rose (1984). A model of neuronal bursting using three coupled first order differential equations. Proc. R. Soc. B 221, 87–102.
where: \(x\): the observed variable; \(\mu\): the Rayleigh nonlinearity
\(\theta\): the pendulum angle

classes.name: Noisy continuous time
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><ellipse cx="28" cy="29" rx="11" ry="7.5"/><path d="M25 21.8 V36.2 M31 21.8 V36.2"/><circle cx="13" cy="28" r="4.5"/><circle cx="12" cy="27" r="1.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M11 24 L8 19 M14.5 23.8 L16 18.5"/><ellipse cx="24" cy="16" rx="4.5" ry="7" transform="rotate(-20 24 16)"/><ellipse cx="32" cy="15.5" rx="4.5" ry="7" transform="rotate(20 32 15.5)"/><path d="M39 29 L43.5 29"/></svg>
classes.motto: Busy as a bee, buzzing along a jittery, noise-driven path.
classes.title: noise-driven continuous-time dynamics
classes.blurb: Stochastic differential equations: wells, resonance, excitability, noisy chaos.

card.description: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, the continuous-time AR(1) and the canonical mean-reverting noise.
card.simulation: Correlation time \(\tau\) log-uniform on [1, 20] samples, at least 50 correlation times per record; subsampled from a fine integration.
references: Uhlenbeck & Ornstein (1930). On the theory of the Brownian motion. Phys. Rev. 36, 823–841.
where: \(x\): the process; \(\tau\): its correlation time (in samples)
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Overdamped Brownian motion in a double-well potential, with noise-driven hopping between the wells (Kramers escape).
equations: dx = (x - x^3)\, dt + \sigma\, dW, \qquad V(x) = x^4/4 - x^2/2
card.simulation: \(\sigma\) stratified over [0.5, 1.1], so there are at least about 30 hops per record.
references: Kramers (1940). Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions. Physica 7, 284–304.
where: \(x\): the particle's position; \(V(x)\): the double-well potential
\(\sigma\): the noise strength
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Noisy normal forms near a bifurcation. Close to criticality the restoring force vanishes, fluctuations grow and slow down (critical slowing down).
equations: \text{pitchfork: } dx = (\mu x - x^3)\, dt + \eta\, dW, \qquad \text{saddle-node: } dx = (\mu - x^2)\, dt + \eta\, dW
\text{Hopf: } dz = \left[(\mu + i\omega) z - |z|^2 z\right] dt + \eta\, dW
card.simulation: Pitchfork, radial and planar Hopf, saddle-node and transcritical forms; \(\kappa = \mu/\eta\) stratified over near-critical (−0.15 to −0.01) and far (−3 to −1) values.
references: Scheffer et al. (2009). Early-warning signals for critical transitions. Nature 461, 53–59.
where: \(x\): the observed state; \(z\): a complex amplitude (Hopf)
\(\mu\): the distance from the bifurcation; \(\eta\): the noise strength; \(\omega\): the Hopf frequency
\(\kappa = \mu/\eta\): the stratified distance to criticality, measured in noise units
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Limit-cycle oscillators with additive noise. The amplitude stays near the cycle while the phase diffuses, so coherence decays over time.
card.simulation: van der Pol with \(\mu\) uniform on [0.3, 3] (even instances) or in its relaxation regime, \(\mu\) on [2, 5], written in Liénard coordinates (odd); noise \(\sigma\) log-stratified over [0.3, 1]; 15–40 samples per period.
references: Pikovsky, Rosenblum & Kurths (2001). Synchronization: A Universal Concept in Nonlinear Sciences. Cambridge University Press.
where: \(\mathbf{u}\): the oscillator's state; \(\mathbf{f}\): its vector field (explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(\sigma\): the noise strength; \(d\mathbf{W}\): independent Wiener increments in each coordinate

card.description: Chaotic flows with dynamical noise, which perturbs the trajectory itself rather than the measurement.
card.simulation: Noise fraction \(\epsilon\) log-uniform on [0.1, 0.5] (capped at 0.06 for Chua, whose double scroll escapes under strong noise); below about 0.02 the noise is invisible against the deterministic motion. Sampled at 8–20 points per period.
references: Crutchfield, Farmer & Huberman (1982). Fluctuations and simple chaotic dynamics. Phys. Rep. 92, 45–82.
where: \(\mathbf{u}\): the flow's state; \(\mathbf{f}\): its vector field (explicit equations are shown for each series)
\(\sigma = \epsilon s\): the dynamical noise strength, a fraction \(\epsilon\) of the attractor's typical size \(s\) (8 for Lorenz, 5 for Rössler, 1.5 for Chua)
\(d\mathbf{W}\), \(\xi(t)\): independent Wiener increments (white noise)
Rössler and Chua: only \(x\) and \(y\) are forced

card.description: A double well with weak periodic forcing and noise. At an optimal noise level the hops lock to the forcing, which is the stochastic resonance effect.
equations: dx = \left(x - x^3 + A\cos\omega t\right) dt + \sigma\, dW
card.simulation: \(\sigma\) stratified around the resonance optimum.
references: Benzi, Sutera & Vulpiani (1981). The mechanism of stochastic resonance. J. Phys. A 14, L453.
Gammaitoni, Hänggi, Jung & Marchesoni (1998). Stochastic resonance. Rev. Mod. Phys. 70, 223–287.
where: \(x\): the particle's position in the double well
\(A, \omega\): the forcing amplitude and angular frequency; \(\sigma\): the noise strength
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Excitable systems driven by noise: at rest they are stable, and noise triggers stereotyped spikes at irregular times. FitzHugh–Nagumo is type-II excitable (a Hopf threshold); the active rotator is type-I (a saddle-node on a circle), so its spikes can come arbitrarily slowly and its rest state is a slow drift.
equations: \text{FitzHugh–Nagumo: } dv = \left(v - v^3/3 - w + I\right) dt + \sigma\, dW, \qquad \epsilon^{-1} dw = (v + a - b w)\, dt
\text{active rotator: } d\varphi = (1 - b \sin\varphi)\, dt + \sigma\, dW, \quad b > 1, \qquad x = -\cos\varphi
card.simulation: FitzHugh–Nagumo with \(I\) stratified over [0, 0.32] and \(\sigma\) log-uniform on [0.15, 0.4] (instances 0–4); active rotator with \(b\) over [1.03, 1.1] and \(\sigma\) uniform on [0.25, 0.35] (5–7).
references: FitzHugh (1961). Impulses and physiological states in theoretical models of nerve membrane. Biophys. J. 1, 445–466.
Lindner, García-Ojalvo, Neiman & Schimansky-Geier (2004). Effects of noise in excitable systems. Phys. Rep. 392, 321–424.
Shinomoto & Kuramoto (1986). Phase transitions in active rotator systems. Prog. Theor. Phys. 75, 1105–1110.
where: \(v\): the fast (voltage-like) variable, observed; \(w\): the slow recovery variable
\(I\): the input current; \(a, b\): the recovery parameters; \(\epsilon\): the time-scale ratio
\(\sigma\): the noise strength
\(\varphi\): the rotator's phase (a spike is a full turn); \(b\): its excitability (the pinning strength)
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Linear relaxation with multiplicative (state-dependent) noise, which gives heavy tails, or driven by colored (OU) noise.
equations: dx = -x\, dt + \xi\, dt, \qquad d\xi = -\xi/\tau_c\, dt + \sqrt{2/\tau_c}\, dW
card.simulation: Multiplicative noise with a small additive floor, \(\sigma\) stratified over [0.5, 1.4] (even instances); OU-colored noise with \(\tau_c\) log-uniform on [0.5, 20] (odd).
references: Hänggi & Jung (1995). Colored noise in dynamical systems. Adv. Chem. Phys. 89, 239–326.
where: \(x\): the observed process; \(\sigma\): the multiplicative noise strength (0.05 is a small additive floor)
\(\xi\): Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (colored) noise with correlation time \(\tau_c\)
\(dW\): Wiener increments

card.description: A noisy heteroclinic cycle of three competing species (rock–paper–scissors dynamics). The state lingers near saddles where one species dominates and switches in a fixed cyclic order.
card.simulation: Symmetric competition, \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\beta = 2\) (instances 0–1), or asymmetric, species-specific \(\alpha_k \in \{0.3, 0.55, 0.8\}\), \(\beta_k \in \{2.4, 1.9, 1.5\}\), so the plateaus differ in length (2). Noise \(\delta\) sets how long each plateau lasts (about \(\ln(1/\delta)\)); observed as \(x_1 + x_2/2\), so the three saddles read as three levels; about 30 dwells per record.
references: May & Leonard (1975). Nonlinear aspects of competition between three species. SIAM J. Appl. Math. 29, 243–253.
where: \(x_k\): the abundance of species \(k = 1, 2, 3\), indices taken cyclically
\(\alpha, \beta\): the competition coefficients
\(\delta\): the noise strength; \(\xi_k\): independent white noises

classes.name: Events and states
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M38 3 V45"/><path d="M40.5 11.5 L43.5 10 M40.5 17.5 L43.5 19"/><circle cx="24" cy="14" r="6"/><circle cx="25.5" cy="13" r="1.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M19.5 10.5 C18.5 5.5 23.5 3.5 26.5 7.5"/><path d="M29.5 12.5 L37 14 L29.5 16"/><path d="M20 18.5 C14 24 14 33 20 37.5 C25 41 30 38 31 32 C32 26 30 21 28 19"/><path d="M26 38.5 L34 45"/><path d="M30.5 29 L37 28 M30 33 L37 33"/></svg>
classes.motto: The woodpecker drums in bursts: rat-a-tat, silence, rat-a-tat-tat.
classes.title: events, point processes, discrete states
classes.blurb: Renewal, self-exciting and Markov processes, read out as real values.

card.description: A renewal process with independent inter-event intervals, observed as the interval sequence.
card.simulation: \(F\) gamma, log-normal, Weibull or Pareto; mean interval stratified over [5, 60]; burstiness \(B\) stratified over [−0.5, 0.8].
references: Goh & Barabási (2008). Burstiness and memory in complex systems. EPL 81, 48002.
where: \(t_k\): the event times; \(\tau_k\): the intervals, drawn independently from \(F\)
\(\mu_\tau, \sigma_\tau\): the mean and standard deviation of the intervals; \(B\): the burstiness

fixed: Exponential kernel \(\phi(s) = (n/d)\, e^{-s/d}\) with decay \(d\); power-law kernel \(\phi(s) = n(\alpha - 1)(1 + s)^{-\alpha}\), \(\alpha = 1.5\)
Read out as a Gaussian-kernel-smoothed event rate (bandwidth given for each series) plus 2% noise
card.description: A self-exciting point process. Each event raises the rate of future events, giving clusters and cascades.
card.simulation: Branching ratio \(n\) stratified over [0.2, 0.98] (upper quarter near-critical); exponential (decay time 2–10) or power-law kernel \(\phi\); mean rate log-uniform on [0.2, 1] per sample; read out as a kernel-smoothed event rate.
references: Hawkes (1971). Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes. Biometrika 58, 83–90.
where: \(\lambda(t)\): the conditional event rate; \(\mu\): the background rate
\(t_k\): past event times; \(\phi\): the excitation kernel
\(n\): the branching ratio (expected offspring per event)

fixed: Spike sizes \(A_n \sim\) U[4, 7] floor s.d.; inter-spike intervals Gamma(4, \(\tau/4\))
card.description: A marked point process on an AR floor: large spikes whose signs follow a third-order rule, so their signs have no pairwise correlation but are dependent in triples.
equations: s_n = -s_{n-1} s_{n-2} r_n, \qquad x_t = \text{AR floor} + \sum_n s_n A_n \mathbb{1}[t = t_n]
card.simulation: Spikes of 4–7 SD at gamma(4) intervals with mean \(\tau\) stratified over [10, 40].
references: Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_n\): the spike times; \(A_n\): the spike sizes; \(s_n = \pm 1\): the spike signs
\(r_n = \pm 1\): independent random signs; \(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\): the indicator function

card.description: Increments of a compound Poisson process with Pareto jumps, zero in most samples, like rainfall totals.
equations: x_t = \sum_{k=1}^{N_t} Y_k, \qquad N_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda), \ \ P(Y > y) \propto y^{-\alpha}
card.simulation: Tail \(\alpha\) stratified over [2.2, 3.5] (finite variance).
references: Cox & Isham (1980). Point Processes. Chapman & Hall.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(N_t\): the number of events in sample \(t\), Poisson with mean \(\lambda\)
\(Y_k\): the jump sizes, Pareto with tail index \(\alpha\)

fixed: Read out as a Gaussian-kernel-smoothed event rate (bandwidth given for each series) plus 2% noise
card.description: A homogeneous Poisson event train read out as a kernel-smoothed firing rate.
card.simulation: Rate \(\lambda\) log-uniform on [0.05, 0.5] per sample.
references: Cox & Isham (1980). Point Processes. Chapman & Hall.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_k\): the event times, a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) per sample
\(K\): the smoothing kernel

fixed: Read out as a Gaussian-kernel-smoothed event rate (bandwidth given for each series) plus 2% noise
card.description: A doubly stochastic (Cox) process, whose Poisson rate is itself a log-normal random process. It is read out as a smoothed rate.
equations: \lambda(t) = \bar\lambda\, e^{s\, u(t)}, \quad u \text{ an OU process}, \qquad x_t = \sum_k K(t - t_k)
card.simulation: OU correlation time log-uniform on [2, 10]; mean rate log-uniform on [0.5, 3].
references: Cox (1955). Some statistical methods connected with series of events. J. R. Stat. Soc. B 17, 129–164.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\lambda(t)\): the random event rate; \(\bar\lambda\): its scale; \(s\): the log-rate scale
\(u(t)\): an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process; \(t_k\): the event times; \(K\): the smoothing kernel

card.description: A discrete Markov chain read out through state-dependent Gaussian emissions, so the series steps between levels with noise.
card.simulation: 2–6 states, mean dwell log-uniform on [2, 40] samples, random or cyclic transitions; \(\sigma\) uniform on [0.15, 0.4].
references: Rabiner (1989). A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proc. IEEE 77, 257–286.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(s_t\): the hidden state (an integer level), a Markov chain
\(\sigma\): the emission noise scale

card.description: Random telegraph noise, a two-state switching signal, in additive Gaussian noise.
equations: x_t = s_t + \sigma \varepsilon_t, \qquad s_t \in \{-1, +1\} \text{ switching at rate } \gamma
card.simulation: \(\gamma\) log-uniform on [0.03, 0.3] per sample; \(\sigma\) uniform on [0.1, 0.4].
references: Gardiner (2009). Stochastic Methods: A Handbook for the Natural and Social Sciences, 4th ed. Springer.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\varepsilon_t\): independent standard Gaussian noise (unless stated otherwise)
\(s_t\): the two-state telegraph signal; \(\gamma\): its switching rate
\(\sigma\): the noise scale

classes.name: Composite and coupled
classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M15 22 C13 7 35 7 33 22 C33 26 30 28 24 28 C18 28 15 26 15 22 Z"/><circle cx="20" cy="20" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="28" cy="20" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M16 25 C10 30 6 30 5 26 C4.5 23 7.5 22 8.5 24"/><path d="M19 27.5 C16 36 11 40 8 38 C6 36 8 34 10 35"/><path d="M24 28 V38 C24 42 27 43 28 41"/><path d="M29 27.5 C32 36 37 40 40 38 C42 36 40 34 38 35"/><path d="M32 25 C38 30 42 30 43 26 C43.5 23 40.5 22 39.5 24"/></svg>
classes.motto: Eight arms, one animal: coupled parts moving as a whole.
classes.title: structured, composite, coupled
classes.blurb: Couplings, mixtures, cross-frequency and cyclostationary structure.

card.description: Dependence only at a long lag: the innovations feed back on themselves \(L\) steps later, then pass through a short AR filter. Short-lag statistics miss it. The nonlinear variant has zero autocorrelation at lag \(L\) but is still dependent there.
equations: u_t = e_t + \phi\, u_{t-L} \quad \text{or} \quad u_t = e_t + \phi\left(\min(u_{t-L}^2, 4) - c\right), \qquad x = \mathrm{AR}(p)[u]
card.simulation: \(L\) stratified over [40, 160], \(|\phi|\) over [0.2, 0.35], a random stable AR(\(p \le 4\)); \(c\) approximately centers the clipped square, so \(\rho(L) \approx 0\) while the dependence at lag \(L\) remains.
where: \(x\): the observed series, an AR(\(p\)) filter applied to \(u\)
\(e_t\): independent Gaussian innovations; \(u_t\): the innovations with long-lag feedback
\(L\): the long lag; \(\phi\): the feedback coefficient; \(c\): the mean of the clipped square

card.description: The dynamics switch every sample with a fixed period: the lag-\(L\) coefficient alternates, so correlation is periodic in time while the variance is not.
card.simulation: \(P = 2\) (even instances) or \(P \in \{3, 4\}\) (odd); \(s(t)\) chosen so every phase has equal variance.
references: Gardner, Napolitano & Paura (2006). Cyclostationarity: half a century of research. Signal Process. 86, 639–697.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(e_t\): independent Gaussian noise
\(L\): the lag; \(\phi(t)\): the lag-\(L\) coefficient, periodic with period \(P\)
\(s(t)\): the noise scale, chosen so every phase has the same variance

card.description: AR(1)-colored noise that replays 15–30% of its own past in segments of 20–60 samples at random lags. The repeats are exact recurrences hidden in noise.
card.simulation: AR(1) color \(\phi\) drawn per series from [0.3, 0.8]; 15–30% of the innovations replayed, in segments of 20–60 samples copied from random earlier positions with fresh noise of 0.05–0.2 SD; the replay is applied to the innovations before filtering, so a replay has no boundary.
references: Eckmann, Kamphorst & Ruelle (1987). Recurrence plots of dynamical systems. Europhys. Lett. 4, 973–977.
Marwan, Romano, Thiel & Kurths (2007). Recurrence plots for the analysis of complex systems. Phys. Rep. 438, 237–329.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(\ell_k\): the lag of replay segment \(k\)
AR(1): an autoregression of order 1 between replays

card.description: Phase–amplitude coupling, as seen in brain rhythms: the amplitude of a fast oscillation is modulated by the phase of a slow one.
card.simulation: Noise \(\sigma = 0.8\), coupling depth 0.6, rhythms with slowly wandering frequency; theta–gamma (narrow and broad band), delta–beta, alpha–gamma, and sleep slow-oscillation–spindle coupling (slow period 100–140 samples, spindle 7–9).
references: Canolty et al. (2006). High gamma power is phase-locked to theta oscillations in human neocortex. Science 313, 1626–1628.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(s_{\text{slow}}, s_{\text{fast}}\): the slow and fast oscillations
\(\theta_{\text{slow}}\): the slow oscillation's phase; \(m\): the modulation depth
\(\sigma\): the noise scale; \(\varepsilon_t\): independent Gaussian noise

card.description: Quadratic phase coupling: three narrowband components whose phases satisfy \(\theta_3 = \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \pi/2\) at every instant. Only the bispectrum detects it; the power spectrum does not.
card.simulation: Frequencies \(f_1, f_2\) drawn from [0.03, 0.18] cycles per sample (\(f_1 + f_2 < 0.45\)); complex Ornstein–Uhlenbeck envelopes with coherence time \(\tau\) log-uniform on [20, 120] samples; noise \(\sigma = 0.5\).
references: Kim & Powers (1979). Digital bispectral analysis and its applications to nonlinear wave interactions. IEEE Trans. Plasma Sci. 7, 120–131.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(a_k(t)\): the amplitudes and \(\theta_k(t)\): the phases of three narrowband components

card.description: Coupled chaotic systems, with coupling stratified across the synchronization transition: Lorenz driving Rössler (the driven system is observed), two mismatched Rösslers (phase synchronization), and a Kaneko coupled map lattice (a ring of 100 logistic-type maps, one site observed) in two regimes: spatiotemporal intermittency and fully developed spatiotemporal chaos.
card.simulation: Flows: coupling \(\varepsilon\) log-stratified over [0.02, 1]. Lattice: \(f(x) = 1 - a x^2\), 100 sites on a ring, 5000 iterations discarded; intermittency at \(a \in [1.78, 1.82]\), \(\varepsilon = 0.3\); spatiotemporal chaos at \(a \in [1.95, 2]\), \(\varepsilon \in [0.03, 0.08]\).
references: Rosenblum, Pikovsky & Kurths (1996). Phase synchronization of chaotic oscillators. Phys. Rev. Lett. 76, 1804.
Kaneko (1989). Pattern dynamics in spatiotemporal chaos. Physica D 34, 1–41.
where: \(\mathbf{u}_1\): the driving system's state; \(\mathbf{u}_2\): the driven system's state
\(\mathbf{f}_2\): the driven system's vector field; \(\mathbf{C}\): the coupling matrix
\(x_n(i)\): the state of lattice site \(i\) at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration; \(f\): the local map, with nonlinearity \(a\)
\(\varepsilon\): the coupling strength (explicit equations are shown for each series)

fixed: Lorenz: \(\sigma = 10\), \(\rho = 28\), \(\beta = 8/3\); Rössler: \(a = b = 0.2\), \(c = 5.7\); the chaotic part is standardized; the seasonal component carries noise of s.d. 0.3
card.description: Additive mixtures of different processes, such as a chaotic flow plus AR noise, a flow under a heavy noise floor, or Rössler plus a seasonal AR.
card.simulation: \(y^{(1)}\) standardized. Lorenz + AR(1) with amplitude ratio \(a\) log-stratified over [0.3, 3]; Lorenz under white noise at SNR −6 to 0 dB; Rössler + a noisy sinusoid; an AR(1) plus telegraph noise.
references: Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y^{(1)}, y^{(2)}\): two independent component processes; \(a\): the amplitude ratio

card.description: On-off intermittency: an invariant state loses transverse stability under chaotic driving, so the response idles near zero and then bursts.
equations: x_{n+1} = a\, \xi_n x_n (1 - x_n), \qquad \xi_n \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1] \text{ (chaotic, from the } r = 4 \text{ logistic map)}
card.simulation: \(a\) just above the threshold \(a = e\), where \(x = 0\) loses transverse stability.
references: Platt, Spiegel & Tresser (1993). On-off intermittency. Phys. Rev. Lett. 70, 279–282.
Heagy, Platt & Hammel (1994). Characterization of on-off intermittency. Phys. Rev. E 49, 1140.
where: \(x_n\): the state at iteration \(n\), one sample per iteration
\(a\): the coupling strength
\(\xi_n\): the chaotic driving signal, uniformly distributed on \([0, 1]\)
