classes.icon: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 48 48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M12 17 L15 8 L20 13 C22 12 26 12 28 13 L33 8 L36 17 C38 24 38 34 24 41 C10 34 10 24 12 17 Z"/><circle cx="19" cy="21" r="4.5"/><circle cx="29" cy="21" r="4.5"/><circle cx="19" cy="21" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><circle cx="29" cy="21" r="1.7" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M22.5 27 L24 30 L25.5 27 Z"/></svg>
classes.motto: The owl reminds us that what we see depends on how we look.
classes.title: observation effects
classes.blurb: What measurement does to a process: clipping, aliasing, gaps, readouts.

card.description: A base process saturated at a fixed level, as when a sensor's range is exceeded.
card.simulation: \(c\) stratified over [0.5, 1.5] SD.
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y_t\): the underlying series; \(\mu, \sigma\): its mean and standard deviation
\(c\): the clipping level, in standard deviations

card.description: A base process with gaps, filled by holding the last value or by linear interpolation.
equations: x_t = y_t \ (t \notin \text{gaps}), \qquad x_t = y_{t_0} \ \text{or linear interpolation across the gap}
card.simulation: Missing fraction uniform on [0.05, 0.4] in gaps of mean length log-uniform on [1, 30]; zero-order hold (even instances) or linear (odd).
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y_t\): the underlying series; \(t_0\): the last observed sample before a gap

card.description: A continuous-time process read at random times, as by an instrument with an irregular sampling clock. The values are recorded in order, one per reading, so the time between samples is itself random.
equations: x_n = y(t_n), \qquad t_{n+1} - t_n = 1 + N_n,\ \ N_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(k - 1)
card.simulation: A continuous-time base process from the collection, generated at \(k\) times the record length (\(k \in \{3, \dots, 6\}\)) and read at 1000 random times with mean spacing \(k\).
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(x_n\): the \(n\)-th recorded value; \(y(t)\): the underlying continuous-time process
\(t_n\): the reading times; \(k\): the mean spacing between readings, in the base process's own samples

card.description: A chaotic flow sampled below its natural resolution, at 2.5–6 points per period, so the waveform aliases.
equations: x_t = u_c(t\,\Delta t), \qquad \Delta t = T/n_p, \ \ n_p \in [2.5, 6]
references: Oppenheim & Schafer (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed. Pearson.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(u_c\): the observed coordinate of a chaotic flow
\(\Delta t\): the sampling interval, \(T/n_p\), with \(T\) the flow's dominant period
\(n_p\): the number of samples per period of the system's dominant oscillation (points per period)

card.description: A chaotic flow sampled densely, so each cycle is resolved smoothly and the record covers only 14–25 periods.
equations: x_t = u_c(t\,\Delta t), \quad \Delta t = T/n_p, \ \ n_p \in [40, 70]
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(u_c\): the observed coordinate of a chaotic flow
\(\Delta t\): the sampling interval, \(T/n_p\), with \(T\) the flow's dominant period
\(n_p\): the number of samples per period of the system's dominant oscillation (points per period)

card.description: A base process observed through a static nonlinearity, which changes the marginal and higher-order statistics but not the underlying dynamics.
equations: x_t = g(y_t), \qquad g \in \{y^2, |y|, e^{y}, y^3\} \ \text{or}\ x_t = y_t y_{t-1}
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y_t\): the underlying series, standardized; \(g\): the static readout function

card.description: A base process with sparse additive outliers of random sign.
card.simulation: Outlier rate uniform on [0.005, 0.05].
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y_t\): the underlying series; \(\sigma_y\): its standard deviation
\(t_k\): the outlier times; \(A_k\): their sizes; \(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\): the indicator function

card.description: A structured base process buried in white measurement noise at or below unit signal-to-noise ratio. White-noise bases are excluded, since white noise plus white noise is still white noise.
references: Kantz & Schreiber (2004). Nonlinear Time Series Analysis, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y_t\): the underlying series; \(\eta_t\): white measurement noise
\(\sigma_y, \sigma_\eta\): their standard deviations; SNR: the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels

card.description: The same stationary process observed at a coarser sampling interval, generated at \(k\) times the length and decimated with an anti-aliasing filter. White-noise bases are excluded, since decimating them leaves only the filter's band-limited noise.
references: Oppenheim & Schafer (2010). Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd ed. Pearson.
Constructed for this collection.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(y\): the underlying process generated at a finer sampling interval
\(h\): the anti-aliasing filter; \(*\): convolution; \(k\): the decimation factor

classes.title: named models of natural and engineered processes
classes.blurb: Models of hearts, brains, climate, ecosystems, lasers and markets.

card.description: Stochastic predator–prey dynamics simulated event by event. Demographic noise from finite populations sustains quasi-cycles that the deterministic model would damp out.
card.simulation: Gillespie SSA; Lotka–Volterra (instances 0–1) or Rosenzweig–MacArthur (2); population scale stratified so demographic noise is visible; prey sampled at fixed intervals.
references: Gillespie (1977). Exact stochastic simulation of coupled chemical reactions. J. Phys. Chem. 81, 2340–2361.
McKane & Newman (2005). Predator–prey cycles from resonant amplification of demographic stochasticity. Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 218102.
where: \(H, P\): the numbers of prey and predators
\(b\): the prey birth rate; \(c\): the predation rate; \(d\): the predator death rate
Each reaction fires at random times (Gillespie's algorithm); \(\varnothing\): removal

fixed: Ricker: carrying capacity \(K = 1\)
Nicholson: 2% multiplicative observation noise
card.description: Nicholson's blowflies, a delayed-feedback population model whose maturation delay drives large, sharp-peaked population cycles (single- and double-peaked here), and the Ricker map with environmental noise.
equations: \dot N = P\, N_\tau\, e^{-N_\tau/N_0} - \delta N, \qquad N_\tau = N(t - \tau)
card.simulation: Blowflies with Gurney–Blythe–Nisbet parameters (\(\delta = 0.175\), \(\tau = 15\), \(P\) stratified over [6, 12]; instance 0) and a longer delay (\(\delta = 0.25\), \(\tau = 20\), \(P\) on [25, 35]; instance 1), both stable limit cycles, with 2% observation noise; Ricker map with \(r\) stratified over [1.8, 3.2] and environmental noise \(\sigma\) on [0.05, 0.3] (2–3).
references: Gurney, Blythe & Nisbet (1980). Nicholson's blowflies revisited. Nature 287, 17–21.
Ricker (1954). Stock and recruitment. J. Fish. Res. Board Can. 11, 559–623.
where: \(N\): the population; \(N_\tau = N(t - \tau)\): its value one maturation delay \(\tau\) ago
\(P\): the maximum per-capita fecundity; \(N_0\): the population scale of density dependence; \(\delta\): the adult death rate
Ricker: \(r\) growth rate, \(K\) carrying capacity, \(\sigma\) environmental noise, \(\varepsilon_t\) Gaussian noise

fixed: Recovery \(\gamma = 1/13\) day\(^{-1}\); latent rate 1/8 day\(^{-1}\) (SEIR); births and deaths \(1/(50 \times 365)\) day\(^{-1}\); immigration 2 per year
Annual seasonal forcing; case counts per 14 days; the first five years discarded
card.description: Seasonally forced stochastic epidemics with births, deaths and immigration, as in measles: multi-annual outbreaks, fade-outs and reintroduction. Observed as fortnightly case counts.
equations: S \xrightarrow{\beta(t) S I / N} I \xrightarrow{\gamma I} R, \qquad \beta(t) = \beta_0\left(1 + \beta_1 \cos 2\pi t\right)
card.simulation: Gillespie SIR (even instances) or SEIR (odd); \(R_0\) log-stratified over [1.5, 15], \(N\) of 50 000 to 1 000 000; five years discarded before the record starts.
references: Keeling & Rohani (2008). Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals. Princeton University Press.
where: \(S, I, R\): the numbers of susceptible, infected and recovered people; \(N\): the population size
\(\beta(t)\): the seasonal transmission rate, with mean \(\beta_0\) and relative amplitude \(\beta_1\); \(t\) in years
\(\gamma\): the recovery rate

card.description: The Bartlett–Lewis rectangular-pulse rainfall model: storms arrive as a Poisson process, each storm spawns rain cells, and each cell is a rectangular pulse. Totals are zero-inflated and heavily right-skewed.
card.simulation: Aggregated to hourly (even instances) or daily (odd) totals; storm rate stratified from temperate to convective regimes.
references: Rodriguez-Iturbe, Cox & Isham (1987). Some models for rainfall based on stochastic point processes. Proc. R. Soc. A 410, 269–288.
where: \(x_t\): the rainfall total in interval \([t, t + \Delta)\)
\(i_c, s_c, d_c\): the intensity, start time and duration of rain cell \(c\)

fixed: Failure threshold 1. Time-predictable: after each quake the stress resets to 0 and a new threshold is drawn with s.d. cv. Slip-predictable: fixed threshold 1, stress drop gamma-distributed with CV cv
Loading noise 30% per sample; 1% measurement noise
card.description: Stress on a fault under steady tectonic loading: a noisy linear ramp that drops at each earthquake, giving an irregular sawtooth. The two variants are time-predictable and slip-predictable recurrence.
card.simulation: Time-predictable (random failure threshold, full drop to a base level; instance 0) or slip-predictable (fixed threshold, random drop; 1); loading rate stratified so about 15–50 cycles fall in the record.
references: Shimazaki & Nakata (1980). Time-predictable recurrence model for large earthquakes. Geophys. Res. Lett. 7, 279–282.
where: \(\sigma(t)\): the stress on the fault; \(\dot\sigma\): the tectonic loading rate
\(\sigma_{\text{base}}, \sigma_{\text{thr}}\): the base and failure-threshold stresses; \(t_k\): the time of the last earthquake
\(\eta_t\): measurement noise

fixed: Aftershock productivity \(\alpha = 1.5\); Omori offset \(c = 0.01\) days; minimum magnitude \(m_0 = 3\); Gutenberg–Richter \(b = 1\), magnitudes capped at 7
\(K\) is set from the branching ratio \(n\): \(K = n(\beta - \alpha)/\beta\) with \(\beta = b \ln 10\)
card.description: The epidemic-type aftershock sequence model: background earthquakes each trigger Omori-law aftershock cascades with Gutenberg–Richter magnitudes. It is the burstiest process in the corpus.
equations: \lambda(t) = \mu + \sum_{t_k < t} K e^{\alpha(m_k - m_0)} (t - t_k + c)^{-p}
card.simulation: Branching ratio stratified over [0.5, 0.95], Omori \(p\) over [1.05, 1.4]; observed as inter-event times.
references: Ogata (1988). Statistical models for earthquake occurrences and residual analysis for point processes. J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 83, 9–27.
where: \(\lambda(t)\): the earthquake rate; \(\mu\): the background rate
\(t_k, m_k\): past earthquake times and magnitudes; \(m_0\): the minimum magnitude
\(K, \alpha\): the aftershock productivity; \(c, p\): the Omori–Utsu decay parameters

card.description: The Barnes model of the sunspot number, an ARMA(2,2) with an 11-year pseudo-period passed through a static nonlinearity that produces the asymmetric cycles.
card.simulation: Semi-annual sampling, so the 11-year pseudo-period is 22 samples (about 45 cycles per record).
references: Barnes, Sargent & Tryon (1980). Sunspot cycle simulation using random noise. In The Ancient Sun, Pergamon, 159–163.
where: \(z_t\): an ARMA(2,2) process with an 11-year pseudo-period
\(y_t\): the observed sunspot-like series

fixed: Hasselmann: a unit-variance OU process plus an annual cycle of amplitude 0.7 (period 12 samples: monthly data)
ENSO: integrated with \(dt = 0.01\) and subsampled to 1000 points; 2% measurement noise
Stommel: \(\eta_1 = 3\), \(\eta_3 = 0.3\); noise s.d. 0.25 on salinity
Daisyworld: albedos 0.75 (white), 0.25 (black), 0.5 (bare ground); daisy death rate 0.3; luminosity noise 0.05, relaxing over 50 time units
card.description: Conceptual stochastic climate models: Hasselmann's red-noise ocean with an annual cycle, the ENSO delayed oscillator driven by weather noise, Stommel's bistable thermohaline circulation, and Daisyworld with noisy luminosity.
card.simulation: One model per instance. Hasselmann \(\tau\) log-uniform on [20, 200] months; ENSO \(\alpha\) stratified over [0.6, 0.95], \(\delta\) uniform on [1.5, 3]; Stommel \(\eta_2\) over [0.6, 1.3]; Daisyworld luminosity over [0.8, 1.2].
references: Hasselmann (1976). Stochastic climate models, Part I. Tellus 28, 473–485.
Suarez & Schopf (1988). A delayed action oscillator for ENSO. J. Atmos. Sci. 45, 3283–3287.
Stommel (1961). Thermohaline convection with two stable regimes of flow. Tellus 13, 224–230.
Watson & Lovelock (1983). Biological homeostasis of the global environment. Tellus B 35, 284–289.
where: \(T\): the temperature anomaly; \(\tau\): the ocean's damping time
\(\alpha\): the delayed-feedback strength; \(\delta\): the delay (ENSO)
\(\sigma\): the weather-noise strength
\(\xi(t)\), \(dW\): Gaussian white noise, the increment of a Wiener process

card.description: Turbulent velocities from the Sabra shell model at a mid-inertial shell (intermittent) and from the randomly forced viscous Burgers equation.
equations: \text{Burgers: } u_t + u u_x = \nu u_{xx} + f(x, t)
\text{Sabra: } \dot u_n = i\left(a k_{n+1} u_{n+2} u^*_{n+1} + b k_n u_{n+1} u^*_{n-1} - c k_{n-1} u_{n-1} u_{n-2}\right) - \nu k_n^2 u_n + f_n
card.simulation: Burgers solved spectrally with 128 modes, observed at a point; Sabra integrated in scalar Python for cross-platform reproducibility.
references: L'vov, Podivilov, Pomyalov, Procaccia & Vandembroucq (1998). Improved shell model of turbulence. Phys. Rev. E 58, 1811.
where: Burgers: \(u(x, t)\) the velocity field, \(\nu\) the viscosity, \(f\) the random forcing; subscripts are partial derivatives
Sabra: \(u_n\) the complex velocity of shell \(n\), \(k_n\) its wavenumber, \(a, b, c\) the interaction coefficients, \(f_n\) the forcing; \({}^*\): complex conjugate

card.description: The Richardson weather generator without its annual cycle, with wet and dry days from a Markov chain and gamma-distributed rainfall on wet days.
card.simulation: \(p_{11}\) stratified over [0.4, 0.8].
references: Richardson (1981). Stochastic simulation of daily precipitation, temperature, and solar radiation. Water Resour. Res. 17, 182–190.
where: \(\text{wet}_t\): whether day \(t\) is wet; \(p_{11}\): the probability a wet day follows a wet day
\(r_t\): the rainfall amount on a wet day, gamma with shape \(k\) and scale \(\theta\)

fixed: Rainfall input: Markov wet/dry days with P(wet | wet) = 0.6 and P(wet | dry) = 0.25, amounts Gamma(0.8, 8)
Baseflow: a slow AR(1) (coefficient 0.995) of 2% of the rain; 2% measurement noise
card.description: Daily river discharge from a Nash cascade of linear reservoirs driven by Markov-gamma rainfall, plus baseflow. Discharge rises sharply after rain and recedes slowly.
equations: Q(t) = \int_0^\infty h(s)\, R(t - s)\, ds + Q_b, \qquad h(s) = \frac{s^{n-1} e^{-s/k}}{k^n \Gamma(n)}
card.simulation: \(n\) stratified over [2, 5], \(k\) uniform on [1, 6] days; no seasonal input.
references: Nash (1957). The form of the instantaneous unit hydrograph. IASH Publ. 45, 114–121.
where: \(Q(t)\): the discharge; \(Q_b\): the baseflow; \(R\): the rainfall input
\(h\): the Nash cascade's response (unit hydrograph); \(n\): the number of reservoirs; \(k\): their time constant
\(\Gamma\): the gamma function

fixed: ON and OFF periods last \(2(1 + \mathrm{Pareto}(\alpha))\) samples; each source's rate is U[0.5, 1.5]
card.description: Network traffic from many ON/OFF sources with heavy-tailed period lengths. Aggregating them gives self-similar packet counts with long-range dependence.
equations: x_t = \sum_{i=1}^{M} r_i\, \mathbb{1}[\text{source } i \text{ ON at } t], \qquad P(\text{ON} > \ell) \propto \ell^{-\alpha},\ \ H = (3 - \alpha)/2
card.simulation: Pareto ON and OFF periods with tail \(\alpha\) stratified over [1.5, 1.9] (\(H\) from 0.55 to 0.75); 150–400 sources, each with its own rate.
references: Willinger, Taqqu, Sherman & Wilson (1997). Self-similarity through high-variability. IEEE/ACM Trans. Netw. 5, 71–86.
where: \(x_t\): the summed rate of the sources active in bin \(t\); \(M\): the number of sources
\(r_i\): source \(i\)'s rate; \(\ell\): an ON-period length; \(\alpha\): the Pareto tail index; \(H\): the resulting Hurst exponent

fixed: Sampling rate 8 kHz; formant bandwidths 80, 100 and 150 Hz, drifting by up to 15%; glottal jitter 2% and shimmer 10%; voiced and unvoiced segments of 200–600 samples
card.description: Source–filter speech: a glottal pulse train (voiced) or noise (unvoiced) through a slowly varying all-pole vocal-tract filter, with voiced/unvoiced switching.
equations: s_t = \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k(t)\, s_{t-k} + g_t, \qquad g_t = \text{Rosenberg pulses (jitter, shimmer) or noise}
card.simulation: 8 kHz equivalent, about 125 ms of signal.
references: Rosenberg (1971). Effect of glottal pulse shape on the quality of natural vowels. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 49, 583–590.
where: \(s_t\): the speech signal; \(a_k(t)\): the vocal-tract filter coefficients (order \(p\)), varying slowly
\(g_t\): the source, a glottal pulse train or noise

fixed: Impulse sizes U[0.7, 1.3]; fault-period jitter 2%
card.description: Vibration of a rotating machine with a bearing fault. Each pass over the defect sends an impulse that rings a structural resonance.
equations: x_t = \sum_k h(t - t_k) + \eta_t, \qquad h(t) = e^{-\zeta\omega_0 t}\sin(\omega_d t),\ \ t_{k+1} - t_k \approx T_f
card.simulation: Fault period \(T_f\) stratified over [15, 60] samples (with jitter), resonance \(Q\) over [5, 30], plus broadband noise.
references: Randall & Antoni (2011). Rolling element bearing diagnostics—a tutorial. Mech. Syst. Signal Process. 25, 485–520.
where: \(x_t\): the observed series, sample \(t = 1, \dots, 1000\)
\(t_k\): the fault impact times; \(T_f\): the fault period; \(h\): the resonance's impulse response
\(\omega_0\): the resonance frequency; \(\zeta\): its damping ratio; \(\omega_d = \omega_0\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}\)
\(\eta_t\): broadband noise

card.description: Collective order parameters near a phase transition, from the Kuramoto model of coupled oscillators and the 2-D Ising model just above its critical temperature.
equations: \text{Ising: } m = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i s_i, \qquad P(\text{flip}) = \min(1, e^{-\Delta E/k_B T})
card.simulation: Kuramoto with \(N = 100\), standard-normal \(\omega_i\), weak phase noise and \(K\) stratified over [0.5, 3], across the synchronization transition at \(K_c \approx 1.6\) (instances 0–1); Metropolis Ising on 32 × 32 at \(T/T_c\) over [1.03, 1.4], the disordered side, where correlations are finite (2).
references: Kuramoto (1984). Chemical Oscillations, Waves, and Turbulence. Springer.
where: Kuramoto: \(\theta_i\) the phase of oscillator \(i\), \(\omega_i\) its natural frequency, \(K\) the coupling, \(N\) the number of oscillators; \(r, \psi\) the order parameter's magnitude (observed) and phase
Ising: \(s_i = \pm 1\) the spins, \(m\) the magnetization (observed), \(\Delta E\) the energy change of a flip, \(k_B T\) the temperature

fixed: Dimensionless Lang–Kobayashi form: delay \(\tau = 1000\), carrier-to-photon lifetime ratio \(T = 1000\), pump \(P = 1\), linewidth factor \(\alpha = 4\)
Spontaneous-emission noise of amplitude \(10^{-3}\); the intensity \(|E|^2\) is sampled every 20 time units
card.description: The Lang–Kobayashi model of a semiconductor laser with delayed optical feedback, in the low-frequency-fluctuation regime: the intensity shows sudden dropouts followed by gradual recovery.
equations: \dot E = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + i\alpha)\, N E + \kappa e^{-i\omega_0\tau} E(t - \tau)
card.simulation: Dimensionless form with \(\alpha = 4\), \(\tau = 1000\), \(T = 1000\), \(P = 1\); feedback \(\kappa\) stratified over [0.08, 0.2]; weak spontaneous-emission noise; intensity \(|E|^2\) observed every 20 time units.
references: Lang & Kobayashi (1980). External optical feedback effects on semiconductor injection laser properties. IEEE J. Quantum Electron. 16, 347–355.
where: \(E\): the complex electric field; \(|E|^2\): the intensity (observed); \(N\): the excess carrier density
\(\alpha\): the linewidth enhancement factor; \(\kappa\): the feedback strength; \(\tau\): the external-cavity delay; \(\omega_0\tau\): the feedback phase
\(T\): the carrier-to-photon lifetime ratio; \(P\): the pump current

card.description: The Oregonator model of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, a stiff relaxation oscillation whose spikes in HBrO\(_2\) span several orders of magnitude.
equations: \epsilon \dot x = q y - x y + x(1 - x), \qquad \epsilon' \dot y = -q y - x y + f z, \qquad \dot z = x - z
card.simulation: \(\epsilon = 0.04\), \(\epsilon' = 0.0004\), \(q = 0.0008\), \(f\) stratified over [0.6, 1.4], inside the oscillatory range (about 0.52 < \(f\) < 2.4); \(\log x\) (HBrO\(_2\)) observed.
references: Field & Noyes (1974). Oscillations in chemical systems. IV. J. Chem. Phys. 60, 1877–1884.
where: \(x, y, z\): scaled concentrations of HBrO\(_2\), Br\(^-\) and the oxidized catalyst
\(\epsilon, \epsilon', q\): the Tyson scaling constants; \(f\): the stoichiometric factor

card.description: Kirman's ant (herding) model: agents switch between two options spontaneously or by recruitment. When recruitment dominates, the population fraction spends long spells near one extreme and switches in bursts.
equations: P(n \to n+1) = \frac{N - n}{N}\left(\varepsilon + k\frac{n}{N-1}\right), \qquad P(n \to n-1) = \frac{n}{N}\left(\varepsilon + k\frac{N-n}{N-1}\right)
card.simulation: \(N = 300\), \(k = 0.5\), \(\varepsilon\) log-uniform on [0.01, 0.05]; observed as \(n/N\) after 3 sweeps per sample.
references: Kirman (1993). Ants, rationality, and recruitment. Q. J. Econ. 108, 137–156.
where: \(n\): the number of agents in state 1; \(N\): the number of agents
\(\varepsilon\): the rate of spontaneous conversion; \(k\): the recruitment rate

card.description: Heartbeat intervals from an integral pulse frequency modulation model: the heart fires each time an integrated, modulated rate reaches threshold. The modulation carries respiratory (HF), Mayer-wave (LF) and 1/f variability.
equations: \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}} \frac{1 + m(t)}{T_0}\, dt = 1, \qquad m = a_{\mathrm{LF}}\sin(2\pi\,0.1 t) + a_{\mathrm{HF}}\sin(2\pi\,0.25 t) + m_{1/f^\beta} + \text{noise}
card.simulation: \(\beta\) stratified over [0.8, 1.3], LF/HF power ratio log-uniform on [0.3, 4], mean interval \(T_0\) uniform on [0.7, 1.1] s; 1000 beats.
references: Bayly (1968). Spectral analysis of pulse frequency modulation in the nervous systems. IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. 15, 257–265.
where: \(t_k\): the heartbeat times; the observed series is the intervals \(t_{k+1} - t_k\)
\(T_0\): the mean interval; \(m(t)\): the modulating signal
\(a_{\mathrm{LF}}, a_{\mathrm{HF}}\): the low- and high-frequency amplitudes; \(m_{1/f^\beta}\): a \(1/f^\beta\) component

card.description: Heartbeat intervals with premature ectopic beats, each a short coupling interval followed by a compensatory pause.
card.simulation: IPFM baseline rhythm; ectopy rate log-uniform on [1, 6]% of beats.
references: Task Force of the ESC and NASPE (1996). Heart rate variability: standards of measurement, physiological interpretation and clinical use. Circulation 93, 1043–1065.
where: \(RR_k\): the \(k\)-th heartbeat interval
\(c\): the coupling-interval fraction of a premature beat

fixed: Concealed conduction: each blocked impulse lengthens the refractory period by 0.02 × prolongation; after each conducted beat it resets to \(\tau_r\) + prolongation × U[0, 1]
card.description: Heartbeat intervals in atrial fibrillation. Chaotic atrial impulses arrive at the AV node as a Poisson stream, and the node conducts only when it is not refractory, giving the irregularly irregular rhythm.
card.simulation: Atrial rate \(\lambda\) stratified over [4, 9] per second; refractory period 0.25–0.45 s, lengthened after each conducted beat and by blocked impulses (concealed conduction).
references: Cohen, Berger & Dushane (1983). A quantitative model for the ventricular response during atrial fibrillation. IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. 30, 769–781.
where: \(t^{\text{atrial}}_j\): the atrial impulse times, a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\)
\(t\): an impulse time; \(t_{\text{last}}\): the last conducted beat; \(\tau_r\): the AV node's refractory period

fixed: Windkessel time constant \(R C\) with \(C = 1.5\); contractile term \(20\, I_{n-1}/0.9\) mmHg; respiratory amplitude \(A = 3\) mmHg
Baroreflex \(f(S) = 18 \arctan((S - 120)/18)\), split 0.4 vagal (next beat) and 0.6 sympathetic (beats 2–5 back); noise s.d. 1 mmHg on pressure, 0.01 s on the interval
card.description: A beat-to-beat model of the baroreflex: systolic pressure, heart interval and peripheral resistance are coupled by a fast vagal and a slow sympathetic feedback, with Windkessel diastolic run-off and respiratory modulation of pressure.
equations: D_n = S_{n-1} e^{-I_{n-1}/(R_{n-1} C)}, \qquad S_n = D_n + \gamma I_{n-1} + A\sin(2\pi t_n/T_{\text{resp}}) + \varepsilon_n
I_n = I_0 + G_v f(S_n) + G_s \textstyle\sum_{j=2}^{5} f(S_{n-j})/4, \qquad f(s) = 18 \arctan\!\left((s - 120)/18\right)
card.simulation: Reflex gain stratified over [6, 18]; respiration period uniform on [3, 5] s; RR observed (instances 0–1) or systolic pressure (2).
references: deBoer, Karemaker & Strackee (1987). Hemodynamic fluctuations and baroreflex sensitivity in humans. Am. J. Physiol. 253, H680–H689.
where: \(S_n, D_n\): the systolic and diastolic pressure of beat \(n\); \(I_n\): the heartbeat interval; \(R_n\): the peripheral resistance
\(C\): the arterial compliance; \(\gamma\): the contractility factor; \(A, T_{\text{resp}}\): the respiratory amplitude and period
\(I_0\): the resting interval; \(G_v, G_s\): the vagal and sympathetic gains; \(f\): the baroreflex response; \(\varepsilon_n\): noise

fixed: RR modulation: Mayer waves (0.1 Hz) amplitude 0.04 and respiration (0.25 Hz) 0.03; R peak normalized to 1 mV; 0.05 mV baseline wander at 0.25 Hz and 0.03 mV noise
card.description: ECGSYN, a synthetic electrocardiogram: a trajectory around a limit cycle with the P, Q, R, S and T waves as Gaussian events, and realistic heart-rate variability.
card.simulation: 20–40 beats per record (log-stratified), RR from IPFM with 0.1 Hz and 0.25 Hz modulation; R peak normalized to 1 mV, plus 0.05 mV respiratory baseline wander and 0.03 mV noise.
references: McSharry, Clifford, Tarassenko & Smith (2003). A dynamical model for generating synthetic electrocardiogram signals. IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. 50, 289–294.
where: \(z\): the ECG voltage (observed); \(z_0\): the baseline
\(\Delta\theta_i\): the angle from wave \(i\)'s position on the limit cycle
\(a_i, b_i\): the amplitude and width of wave \(i \in \{P, Q, R, S, T\}\)

fixed: Dimensionless: \(P = 1\), \(V_{\max} = 1.5\), \(\theta = 1\), \(n = 6\)
Observed: a breathing waveform with period 8 samples and depth \(0.2 + V\); breath-to-breath jitter of 10% in rate and 8% in depth
card.description: The chemoreflex loop with a circulatory delay, a Mackey–Glass-type model of breathing control. Long delays destabilize it into Cheyne–Stokes periodic breathing.
equations: \dot C = P - V(C(t - \tau))\, C, \qquad V(C) = V_{\max}\frac{C^n}{\theta^n + C^n}
card.simulation: The ventilation drive modulates the amplitude of a breathing waveform; delay \(\tau\) stratified from stable to periodic breathing.
references: Mackey & Glass (1977). Oscillation and chaos in physiological control systems. Science 197, 287–289.
where: \(C\): the blood CO\(_2\) concentration; \(P\): its production rate
\(V\): the ventilation, responding to \(C\) a circulatory delay \(\tau\) earlier
\(V_{\max}, \theta, n\): the ventilatory response's maximum, threshold and steepness

fixed: Wilson–Cowan: couplings \(w_{EE}, w_{EI}, w_{IE}, w_{II} = 16, 12, 15, 3\); thresholds 5 (E) and 12 (I); time constant 0.1; noise s.d. 0.15
Epileptor: the constants of Jirsa et al. (2014); noise s.d. 0.025 on the fast subsystem and 0.25 on the second
card.description: Neural-mass models of EEG: Jansen–Rit cortical columns (alpha rhythm, spike-and-wave), noisy Wilson–Cowan populations, and the Epileptor, which cycles through seizure onset and offset, or, just below its seizure threshold, spikes interictally without seizing.
equations: \text{Jansen–Rit: } \ddot y_i = A a\, S_i(\cdot) - 2a\dot y_i - a^2 y_i, \qquad S(v) = \frac{2e_0}{1 + e^{r(v_0 - v)}}
card.simulation: Jansen–Rit input \(p\) stratified across noise-driven alpha, 3 Hz spike-wave and high-input regimes; sampled at about 250 Hz equivalent.
references: Jansen & Rit (1995). Electroencephalogram and visual evoked potential generation in a mathematical model of coupled cortical columns. Biol. Cybern. 73, 357–366.
Wilson & Cowan (1972). Excitatory and inhibitory interactions in localized populations of model neurons. Biophys. J. 12, 1–24.
Jirsa et al. (2014). On the nature of seizure dynamics. Brain 137, 2210–2230.
where: Jansen–Rit: \(y_i\) the postsynaptic potentials, \(A\) the synaptic gain, \(a\) the inverse time constant, \(S\) the sigmoid with maximum \(2e_0\), slope \(r\) and threshold \(v_0\)
Wilson–Cowan: \(E, I\) the excitatory and inhibitory activities, \(\tau_E\) the time constant, \(w\) the coupling weights, \(P\) the input, \(\sigma\xi\) noise

card.description: Single-neuron models with noisy input current: Hodgkin–Huxley (tonic, and just below rheobase, where noise-induced spikes interrupt subthreshold oscillations), Izhikevich (regular spiking, chattering and a thalamo-cortical cell near threshold), Morris–Lecar and Hindmarsh–Rose bursting.
equations: \text{Izhikevich: } \dot v = 0.04 v^2 + 5v + 140 - u + I, \quad \dot u = a(bv - u), \quad v \ge 30 \Rightarrow v \leftarrow c,\ u \leftarrow u + d
\text{Hodgkin–Huxley: } C\dot V = I - g_{\mathrm{Na}} m^3 h (V - E_{\mathrm{Na}}) - g_{\mathrm{K}} n^4 (V - E_{\mathrm{K}}) - g_L (V - E_L)
card.simulation: Membrane potential observed. Input currents above threshold for most instances; Hodgkin–Huxley near rheobase (\(I\) on [5.8, 6.2], weak noise) and the Izhikevich thalamo-cortical cell (\(I\) on [1.5, 2.5]) fire sparsely and irregularly.
references: Hodgkin & Huxley (1952). A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve. J. Physiol. 117, 500–544.
Izhikevich (2003). Simple model of spiking neurons. IEEE Trans. Neural Netw. 14, 1569–1572.
where: Izhikevich: \(v\) the membrane potential (mV), \(u\) the recovery variable, \(I\) the input current, \(a, b, c, d\) the model parameters
Hodgkin–Huxley: \(V\) the membrane potential, \(C\) the capacitance, \(m, h, n\) the gating variables, \(g\) the conductances, \(E\) the reversal potentials

fixed: \(p_1 = 0.03\) min\(^{-1}\) (0.015 for the insulin-resistant series), \(p_2 = 0.02\) min\(^{-1}\); \(G_b = 90\) mg/dL, \(I_b = 10\) µU/mL
Insulin clearance 0.14 min\(^{-1}\), secretion 0.005 per mg/dL of glucose above 80, acting after a 30-min delay; insulin noise s.d. 0.3
Meals every 180–420 min (the first at 300–500 min), each a gamma-shaped appearance pulse peaking 30 min after the meal, of size U[2, 5] mg/dL/min
Glucose sampled every 5 min; the first day is discarded
card.description: Blood glucose from the Bergman minimal model, driven by meals at irregular times and by an ultradian oscillation from delayed insulin action.
equations: \dot G = -(p_1 + X) G + p_1 G_b + R_a(t), \qquad \dot X = -p_2 X + p_3 (I - I_b)
card.simulation: Meals every 3–7 h as gamma-shaped glucose appearance pulses (peak 2–5 mg/dL/min, so post-meal glucose peaks near 150–250 mg/dL); Sturis-type ultradian oscillation; one instance insulin-resistant (\(p_3 = 3 \times 10^{-6}\), \(p_1 = 0.015\)), with larger, slower excursions; sampled every 5 min over about 3.5 days.
references: Bergman, Ider, Bowden & Cobelli (1979). Quantitative estimation of insulin sensitivity. Am. J. Physiol. 236, E667–E677.
Sturis, Polonsky, Mosekilde & Van Cauter (1991). Computer model for mechanisms underlying ultradian oscillations of insulin and glucose. Am. J. Physiol. 260, E801–E809.
where: \(G\): plasma glucose; \(G_b\): its basal level; \(R_a(t)\): the glucose appearance from meals
\(X\): insulin action; \(I, I_b\): plasma insulin and its basal level
\(p_1\): glucose effectiveness; \(p_2, p_3\): the insulin-action rate constants

fixed: Kronauer: light drive 0.3 L for 16 h a day (lights on at 07:00, jittered by up to ±4 h for the melatonin series); daily light intensity \(L \sim\) U[0.25, 1]; oscillator noise 0.01
Hormone: Weibull(2.5) pulse intervals, Gamma(2, 1) pulse masses; 5% measurement noise
card.description: Circadian and pulsatile physiology: the Kronauer circadian pacemaker, a higher-order van der Pol-type limit-cycle oscillator entrained by a light–dark cycle, and pulsatile hormone secretion with exponential clearance.
equations: \dot x = \tfrac{\pi}{12}\left[x_c + \mu\left(\tfrac{x}{3} + \tfrac{4}{3}x^3 - \tfrac{256}{105}x^7\right) + B\right], \qquad \dot x_c = \tfrac{\pi}{12}\left[q B x_c - x\left(\left(\tfrac{24}{0.99669\,\tau_x}\right)^2 + k B\right)\right]
\text{hormone: } c(t) = \sum_k M_k\, e^{-(t - t_k)/\tau_c}, \qquad t_k \text{ renewal pulses}
card.simulation: Circadian model sampled hourly with \(\tau_x\) stratified over [23.5, 25] h and day-to-day variation in light intensity (instance 0); the same pacemaker under an irregular light schedule, read out as a melatonin-like nocturnal pulse (1); pulsatile secretion with gamma pulse masses sampled every 10 min (2–3).
references: Jewett, Forger & Kronauer (1999). Revised limit cycle oscillator model of human circadian pacemaker. J. Biol. Rhythms 14, 493–499.
Keenan & Veldhuis (1998). A biomathematical model of time-delayed feedback in the human male hypothalamic–pituitary–Leydig cell axis. Am. J. Physiol. 275, E157–E176.
where: \(x, x_c\): the circadian pacemaker's state (\(x\) observed); \(\mu = 0.13\): its stiffness; \(\tau_x\): its intrinsic period in hours; \(B\): the light drive; \(q = 1/3\), \(k = 0.55\): the light-coupling constants
\(c(t)\): the hormone concentration; \(t_k, M_k\): the secretion pulse times and masses; \(\tau_c\): the clearance time

fixed: Telegraph model: mRNA degradation \(\gamma = 0.1\); protein translation \(k_p = 2\), dilution \(\gamma_p = 0.2\); sampled every unit of time
Goldbeter: channel noise \(0.3\sqrt{|u|}\); 2% measurement noise
card.description: Noise and oscillations inside cells: bursty telegraph-model transcription simulated molecule by molecule and read out as protein, and noisy calcium-induced calcium release oscillations.
equations: \text{telegraph: } G_{\text{off}} \underset{k_{\text{off}}}{\overset{k_{\text{on}}}{\rightleftharpoons}} G_{\text{on}} \xrightarrow{k} G_{\text{on}} + M, \quad M \xrightarrow{\gamma} \varnothing, \qquad p_{t+1} = p_t + k_p M_t - \gamma_p p_t
\text{Goldbeter: } \dot Z = v_0 + v_1\beta - v_2(Z) + v_3(Z, Y) + k_f Y - k Z, \quad \dot Y = v_2(Z) - v_3(Z, Y) - k_f Y
card.simulation: Telegraph transcription by Gillespie SSA (\(k_{\text{on}}\) log-stratified over [0.05, 0.3]), with protein translated from the mRNA count and diluted (lifetime about 5 samples; four instances); the Goldbeter model with stimulation \(\beta\) stratified over [0.3, 0.9] and intrinsic channel noise (two instances).
references: Peccoud & Ycart (1995). Markovian modeling of gene-product synthesis. Theor. Popul. Biol. 48, 222–234.
Goldbeter, Dupont & Berridge (1990). Minimal model for signal-induced Ca²⁺ oscillations. PNAS 87, 1461–1465.
where: Telegraph: \(G_{\text{on}}, G_{\text{off}}\) the gene's states, switching at rates \(k_{\text{on}}, k_{\text{off}}\); \(M\) the mRNA molecules, \(k\) the transcription rate, \(\gamma\) the degradation rate; \(p\) the protein level (observed), \(k_p\) its translation rate, \(\gamma_p\) its dilution rate
Goldbeter: \(Z\) cytosolic Ca²⁺ (observed), \(Y\) Ca²⁺ in the internal store, \(\beta\) the stimulation; \(v_2, v_3\) the pumping and release fluxes

fixed: Gait: 1.1 s + 0.03 × fGn
EMG: envelope \(0.1 + \max(0, \sin 2\pi t/P)^2\) times Gaussian noise
Tremor: an AR(2) resonance with pole radius 0.97, plus white noise of s.d. 0.5
card.description: Movement physiology, including stride intervals with fractal fluctuations, surface EMG gated by the gait cycle, and physiological tremor.
equations: \text{stride: } I_n = 1.1\,\mathrm{s} + 0.03\, \epsilon^{(H)}_n, \qquad \text{EMG: } x_t = a(t)\, \varepsilon_t,\ a(t) \text{ a bursting envelope}
card.simulation: Stride-interval \(H\) stratified over [0.6, 0.9] (two instances); tremor as 8–12 Hz narrowband noise at 100 Hz sampling.
references: Hausdorff et al. (1995). Is walking a random walk? Evidence for long-range correlations in stride interval of human gait. J. Appl. Physiol. 78, 349–358.
where: \(I_n\): the \(n\)-th stride interval; \(\epsilon^{(H)}_n\): fractional Gaussian noise with Hurst exponent \(H\)
EMG: \(\varepsilon_t\) a Gaussian carrier, \(a(t)\) the muscle-activation envelope
